Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.w: Fundamental Rule 8 requires firms to prepare for resolution, ensuring an orderly process in the event of failure.

n.1: Fundamental Rule 3 is about prudence, not failure planning.
n.2: Fundamental Rule 4 concerns financial resources, not resolution planning.
n.3: Fundamental Rule 5 relates to risk systems, not failure planning.
n.4: Fundamental Rule 6 concerns organisation, not failure readiness.

Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.q: Which PRA Fundamental Rule requires firms to organise and control their affairs responsibly?
Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.w: PRA Fundamental Rule 6 requires firms to organise and control their affairs responsibly, with adequate risk management systems and resources.

n.1: Fundamental Rule 2 relates to diligence, not organisational control.
n.2: Fundamental Rule 3 requires prudence, not organisation.
n.3: Fundamental Rule 4 concerns financial resources, not organisation.
n.4: Fundamental Rule 8 covers preparing for resolution, not ongoing organisation.

Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.q: What type of sanctions can regulators apply to individuals guilty of insider dealing?
Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.w: Insider dealing can attract civil sanctions (fines, injunctions) under FCA rules and criminal sanctions (imprisonment, fines) under CJA 1993.

n.1: Warnings alone would not deter insider dealing.
n.2: Training requirements are not a sanction for insider dealing.
n.3: Restitution is not the primary sanction for insider trading.
n.4: Restrictions on advice do not address insider dealing directly.

Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.q: Which of the following best describes the FCA’s approach to regulation under FSMA?
o: Principles-based regulation supported by detailed rules
Rigid rulebook with no reliance on principles
Delegation of rule-making to HM Treasury
Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.w: The FCA applies a principles-based framework, setting high-level Principles for Businesses alongside detailed COBS, DISP, and other rules.

n.1: The FCA does not operate solely by rigid rulebook; it balances principles with rules.
n.2: Prudential supervision is primarily PRA’s responsibility, not FCA’s.
n.3: The FCA regulates both retail and wholesale markets, not just wholesale.
n.4: HM Treasury sets legislation but does not draft FCA’s detailed rules.

Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.q: Which FCA operational objective is most directly linked to ensuring consumers are treated fairly when purchasing financial products?
Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.w: The consumer protection objective requires the FCA to secure an appropriate degree of protection for consumers, including fair treatment in product sales.

n.1: Market integrity deals with trust in the system, not direct consumer fairness.
n.2: Competition focuses on market dynamics, not fairness of treatment.
n.3: Prudential safety is the PRA’s remit, not FCA’s.
n.4: Policyholder protection is specific to PRA’s insurance role.

Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.q: What is the FCA’s approach when firms self-report breaches promptly and cooperate fully?
o: They are automatically exempt from enforcement
They must face the same sanctions regardless
They are referred directly to the CPS
They are fined the maximum amount by default
Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.w: Firms that self-report and cooperate may benefit from reduced sanctions, reflecting the FCA’s emphasis on transparency and remediation.

n.1: Exemption is not guaranteed; sanctions may still apply.
n.2: The FCA uses proportionality, not identical sanctions regardless of cooperation.
n.3: Referral to CPS occurs in criminal cases, not every breach.
n.4: Maximum fines are reserved for the most serious, uncooperative breaches.

Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.q: Which PRA Fundamental Rule requires firms to act with integrity?
Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.w: Fundamental Rule 1 requires firms to conduct their business with integrity, serving as a foundation for prudential supervision.

n.1: Fundamental Rule 2 requires diligence, not integrity.
n.2: Fundamental Rule 3 covers prudence, not integrity.
n.3: Fundamental Rule 5 is about risk management, not integrity.
n.4: Fundamental Rule 6 requires organisation and control, not integrity.

Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.q: Which PRA Fundamental Rule requires firms to maintain adequate capital and liquidity resources?
Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.w: Fundamental Rule 4 requires firms to maintain adequate financial and non-financial resources, including capital and liquidity buffers.

n.1: Fundamental Rule 2 covers diligence, not resources.
n.2: Fundamental Rule 3 focuses on prudence, not resources.
n.3: Fundamental Rule 5 is about risk systems, not resources directly.
n.4: Fundamental Rule 7 is about regulator cooperation, not resources.

Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.q: Which body has the power to prosecute criminal insider dealing cases in the UK?
Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.w: The FCA investigates insider dealing but criminal prosecutions are brought by the Crown Prosecution Service under the Criminal Justice Act 1993.

n.1: The FCA can prosecute some offences but typically refers serious criminal cases to CPS.
n.2: The PRA does not prosecute criminal cases; it is a prudential regulator.
n.3: HM Treasury sets legislation, not prosecutions.
n.4: The CMA deals with competition law, not insider dealing.

Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.q: What is meant by the FCA’s market integrity objective?
o: Protecting and enhancing confidence and stability in the financial system
Guaranteeing profits for all authorised firms
Administering monetary policy in the UK
Issuing deposit insurance to all consumers
Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.w: The market integrity objective is to protect and enhance confidence, resilience, and stability in the UK financial system.

n.1: The FCA does not guarantee firm profitability; its concern is market confidence.
n.2: Monetary policy is the Bank of England’s role, not FCA’s.
n.3: Fiscal management is for HM Treasury, not FCA.
n.4: Deposit insurance is provided through FSCS, not directly by the FCA.

Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.q: What does the FCA’s consumer protection objective require it to secure?
o: An appropriate degree of protection for consumers
The elimination of all consumer risk
Universal access to free financial advice
Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.w: The FCA’s consumer protection objective is to secure an appropriate degree of protection for consumers in regulated markets.

n.1: Regulation cannot eliminate all risk; it ensures proportionate protection.
n.2: Compensation schemes like FSCS cover specific cases, not all investor losses.
n.3: Insurance is not provided by the FCA; it regulates insurers instead.
n.4: Free financial advice is not a statutory requirement.

Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.q: What is the role of HM Treasury in relation to the FCA and PRA objectives?
o: It sets the legislative framework within which the regulators operate
Financial Regulators’ Responsibilities.w: HM Treasury sets the legislative and policy framework, giving regulators their statutory objectives and ensuring accountability to Parliament.

n.1: Individual firm supervision is done by FCA or PRA, not HM Treasury.
n.2: Consumer disputes are handled by FOS, not HM Treasury.
n.3: Interest rates are set by the Bank of England’s MPC.
n.4: Guaranteeing products is not a Treasury function.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which factor distinguishes actual authority from apparent authority in agency law?
o: Actual authority is granted by the principal; apparent authority arises from third-party perception
Actual authority arises only in emergencies; apparent authority is always implied
Apparent authority is written; actual authority is always oral
Actual authority requires ratification; apparent authority does not
Apparent authority is only relevant in partnership law
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Actual authority derives directly from the principal’s express or implied grant; apparent authority arises when a third party reasonably relies on a representation of authority.

n.1: Agency by necessity relates to emergencies, not actual authority.
n.2: Authority can be written or oral; this distinction is incorrect.
n.3: Actual authority does not require ratification; it is valid when granted.
n.4: Apparent authority applies across agency law, not just partnerships.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: What is the legal effect of a marriage on an existing will in England and Wales?
o: It revokes the will unless made in contemplation of marriage
It automatically amends the will to include the new spouse
It has no effect on the existing will
It only revokes bequests to former partners
It revokes only those clauses relating to property
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Marriage revokes a will unless it is expressly made in contemplation of that marriage under the Wills Act 1837.

n.1: The law does not automatically amend wills; new wills must be drafted.
n.2: Marriage does affect an existing will, except when made in contemplation of it.
n.3: Revocation is not limited to bequests to former partners; the whole will is revoked.
n.4: Revocation applies to the whole will, not just property clauses.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following best describes ownership under a trust arrangement?
o: Trustees hold legal title, beneficiaries hold equitable interest
Beneficiaries hold both legal and equitable title
Settlor retains legal ownership after creating the trust
The trust itself is a legal person owning the assets
Trustees and beneficiaries share legal ownership jointly
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Trust law separates ownership: trustees hold legal title, while beneficiaries enjoy equitable ownership.

n.1: Beneficiaries do not hold legal title; trustees administer the trust.
n.2: The settlor usually gives up legal ownership when establishing the trust.
n.3: A trust is not itself a legal person; ownership vests in trustees.
n.4: Trustees hold sole legal title; beneficiaries have rights in equity, not joint legal ownership.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which statement correctly describes wrongful trading under the Insolvency Act?
o: Directors can be held personally liable if they continue trading when insolvency is unavoidable
Shareholders are liable for company debts if dividends are paid
Creditors are liable if they accept repayment from insolvent companies
Auditors are liable for failing to detect insolvency
Employees are liable if they continue to work for an insolvent company
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Wrongful trading occurs when directors knew or ought to have known there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvency but continued trading, risking personal liability.

n.1: Shareholders’ liability is limited to unpaid share capital, not wrongful trading.
n.2: Creditors are not liable for accepting payments; the issue is director conduct.
n.3: Auditors may face negligence claims but are not liable under wrongful trading provisions.
n.4: Employees are not personally liable for insolvency decisions.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which statutory duty requires directors to act in the interests of creditors once insolvency is likely?
o: Directors’ duty to avoid wrongful trading
Duty to promote the success of the company
Duty to declare interests in transactions
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: When insolvency is likely, directors must prioritise creditors’ interests, avoiding wrongful trading to prevent personal liability.

n.1: This duty applies generally but shifts to creditors’ interests when insolvency threatens.
n.2: Acting within powers is a Companies Act duty but not specific to insolvency.
n.3: Declaring interests is a governance duty, not insolvency-specific.
n.4: Maintaining registers is administrative, not related to insolvency.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following describes the role of a guardian appointed in a will?
o: They care for minor children if both parents die
They manage trust property for beneficiaries
They distribute estate assets to creditors
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Guardians appointed in wills are responsible for the care of minor children if both parents die while the children are under 18.

n.1: Trustees, not guardians, manage trust property.
n.2: Executors, not guardians, distribute estate assets.
n.3: Codicils amend wills; guardians have no drafting powers.
n.4: Intestacy rules are fixed by statute, not by guardians.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which best describes equitable ownership of property?
o: The right to benefit from property even if legal title is held by another
The ability to enforce contracts in one’s own name
The statutory title to land registered at HM Land Registry
The absolute right to dispose of property regardless of legal title
Ownership rights limited to personal property only
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Equitable ownership arises where one party enjoys the benefits of property, though another holds the legal title, as in trusts and nominee arrangements.

n.1: Contract enforcement relates to legal standing, not equitable ownership.
n.2: Legal title to land is registered, but equitable interests may not be.
n.3: Equitable owners cannot always dispose freely without legal titleholder cooperation.
n.4: Equitable interests apply to land and personal property, not just personal property.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: What is the maximum period allowed for private trusts under the perpetuity rules?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The Perpetuities and Accumulations Act 2009 sets the maximum duration of private trusts at 125 years.

n.1: 50 years is too short; the statutory maximum is longer.
n.2: 80 years was used historically but has been extended.
n.3: 100 years is not the current statutory limit.
n.4: 150 years exceeds the statutory maximum.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which trust type provides beneficiaries with a fixed entitlement to income or capital?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: An interest in possession trust gives a beneficiary the right to trust income or assets, unlike a discretionary trust where trustees decide distributions.

n.1: Discretionary trusts give no fixed entitlement to beneficiaries.
n.2: Bare trusts transfer property to beneficiaries once conditions are met.
n.3: Protective trusts restrict beneficiaries’ access, not guarantee fixed entitlements.
n.4: Constructive trusts are imposed by law, not created for fixed entitlements.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which UK insolvency process allows small companies to obtain a moratorium while they consider a rescue plan?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Small companies may apply for a CVA with moratorium, giving protection from creditor action while proposals are considered.

n.1: Debt Relief Orders apply only to individuals.
n.2: Administration applies to companies generally but is not specific to small companies’ CVA moratorium.
n.3: Compulsory liquidation winds up the company; it is not a rescue measure.
n.4: Receivership benefits secured creditors, not rescue plans.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Under intestacy rules, who inherits if a deceased has no surviving spouse, children, or parents?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: If there is no spouse, child, or parent, the estate passes to siblings, then to wider relatives if none survive.

n.1: Friends are not recognised under statutory intestacy rules.
n.2: Local authorities do not inherit estates under intestacy.
n.3: Executors only administer estates; they do not inherit unless named beneficiaries.
n.4: The Insolvency Service does not administer intestate estates.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which rule prevents beneficiaries from inheriting if they predecease the testator?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The doctrine of lapse means a gift fails if the beneficiary dies before the testator, unless a substitution or statutory saving provision applies.

n.1: The rule against perpetuities limits trust duration, not predeceasing beneficiaries.
n.2: The forfeiture rule bars inheritance by unlawful killers, not predeceased heirs.
n.3: Saunders v Vautier allows trust termination, not lapse.
n.4: Privity governs contracts, not succession.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: What is the effect if a witness to a will is also a beneficiary?
o: The gift to the witness is void, but the rest of the will remains valid
The will must be re-executed with new witnesses
The witness automatically becomes an executor
The gift is doubled to prevent conflict of interest
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: If a witness or their spouse is a beneficiary, the will itself remains valid but the specific gift to the witness fails.

n.1: The will is not invalidated entirely; only the gift is affected.
n.2: The will does not need re-execution; it remains valid with the invalid gift removed.
n.3: Witnessing does not confer executorship.
n.4: There is no rule that gifts increase if a witness is involved.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following is true regarding a codicil?
o: It amends an existing will without replacing it
It automatically revokes the original will
It is only valid if handwritten by the testator
It can be witnessed by one person only
It is valid only if registered at the Probate Registry
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A codicil is a legal document that amends or adds to a will, without replacing the entire will, and must meet the same formal requirements as a will.

n.1: A codicil does not revoke the original will; it supplements or amends it.
n.2: Codicils may be typed or printed; handwriting is not required.
n.3: A codicil must be witnessed by two people, like a will.
n.4: Registration is not mandatory for validity in England and Wales.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following is the role of a trustee?
o: To manage trust property for the benefit of beneficiaries
To draft the original trust deed
To decide succession rules under intestacy
To provide probate services for executors
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Trustees hold and manage trust property in accordance with the trust deed for the benefit of beneficiaries, exercising fiduciary duties.

n.1: The settlor or solicitor drafts the trust deed, not the trustees.
n.2: Inheritance under intestacy follows statutory rules, not trusteeship.
n.3: Succession rules under intestacy are fixed by statute, not trustees.
n.4: Executors administer estates, not trustees unless appointed separately.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which insolvency process allows a secured creditor to appoint a receiver to realise assets subject to a fixed or floating charge?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Receivership enables a secured creditor to appoint a receiver to realise charged assets and repay their debt.

n.1: Liquidation winds up the company but is not initiated by secured creditors directly.
n.2: A CVA is a compromise with creditors, not enforcement of security.
n.3: Debt Relief Orders apply to individuals, not companies.
n.4: Administration aims to rescue the business, not specifically enforce security.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which insolvency procedure allows an individual to repay debts over time under court approval, avoiding bankruptcy?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: An IVA is a formal agreement approved by creditors and the court, allowing repayment of debts over time and avoiding bankruptcy.

n.1: Debt Relief Orders apply to low-level debtors with minimal assets, not general repayment arrangements.
n.2: Compulsory liquidation applies to companies, not individuals.
n.3: Receivership relates to secured creditors enforcing charges, not individual debtors.
n.4: Administration orders are for companies, not individuals.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which best describes ownership of assets in a discretionary trust?
o: Trustees hold legal title; beneficiaries’ rights depend on trustee discretion
Beneficiaries hold both legal and beneficial ownership
Settlor retains legal ownership after establishing the trust
Trustees acquire both legal and beneficial ownership
The trust itself owns the assets as a legal person
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Trustees hold legal title, while beneficiaries only have a right to be considered for distributions at trustees’ discretion.

n.1: Beneficiaries lack fixed beneficial ownership in discretionary trusts.
n.2: The settlor usually gives up ownership when creating the trust.
n.3: Trustees do not obtain beneficial ownership; they administer assets for beneficiaries.
n.4: A trust is not itself a separate legal entity.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following best describes the principle of privity of contract?
o: Only parties to a contract can enforce it
Third parties can always enforce contracts that benefit them
Regulators can enforce any contract within their remit
Courts may enforce contracts regardless of parties’ consent
Contracts must be written to be enforceable
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The doctrine of privity means only parties to a contract have enforceable rights and obligations under it, subject to statutory exceptions.

n.1: Third parties cannot automatically enforce contracts unless the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 applies.
n.2: Regulators do not acquire contract enforcement powers by default; they enforce rules, not private contracts.
n.3: Courts enforce contracts between parties; they do not impose obligations without contractual consent.
n.4: Contracts may be oral or implied; writing is not a universal requirement.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following terms describes the remainder of an estate after debts, taxes, and specific gifts are distributed?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The residue is what remains of the estate once debts, taxes, and all specific and pecuniary legacies have been settled.

n.1: Pecuniary legacies are fixed sums of money, not the remainder.
n.2: A specific devise is a gift of real property, not the residual estate.
n.3: A codicil is a will amendment, not the remainder of an estate.
n.4: A life interest gives a person rights during their lifetime, not the whole residue.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which statutory mechanism allows creditors to challenge transactions intended to put assets beyond their reach before insolvency?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Transactions at undervalue can be challenged if a debtor disposed of assets for less than fair value prior to insolvency, prejudicing creditors.

n.1: Floating charge rules govern security ranking, not asset disposal.
n.2: Frustration deals with contract discharge, not insolvency.
n.3: Promissory estoppel prevents denying promises, not asset transfers.
n.4: Set-off offsets mutual debts, not fraudulent asset transfers.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which type of charge requires registration at Companies House to be valid against a liquidator?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Both fixed and floating charges must be registered at Companies House to be enforceable against a liquidator or administrator.

n.1: Fixed charges alone are not the only ones requiring registration.
n.2: Floating charges also require registration.
n.3: Preferential creditors do not rely on charges; they have statutory priority.
n.4: Unsecured creditors cannot register charges; their claims are unsecured.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following best defines a pecuniary legacy?
o: A gift of money under a will
A gift of land or property
A share of the residue of an estate
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A pecuniary legacy is a fixed monetary gift left in a will, such as £10,000 to a named person.

n.1: Personal possessions are specific legacies, not pecuniary ones.
n.2: Land or property gifts are specific devises, not pecuniary.
n.3: Residue gifts are residuary legacies, not pecuniary.
n.4: Trusts for minors are not pecuniary legacies.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which term describes a gift in a will of a specific item such as jewellery?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A specific legacy is a gift of a particular identifiable item, such as jewellery or a property, under a will.

n.1: Pecuniary legacies are gifts of money, not items.
n.2: Residuary bequests gift what remains after other legacies and debts are paid.
n.3: Demonstrative legacies are money gifts from a specific source.
n.4: General bequests are non-specific gifts, not tied to an identified item.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which statement best distinguishes assignment from novation when transferring a client’s service agreement to a new provider?
o: Assignment transfers rights only; novation transfers rights and obligations with all parties’ consent
Assignment and novation both transfer rights and obligations automatically
Assignment requires all parties’ consent; novation does not
Novation transfers rights only; assignment transfers obligations
Neither can be used for service agreements
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Assignment passes contractual rights (e.g., to payment) but not burdens; novation substitutes a new party, transferring both rights and obligations with tri-party consent.

n.1: Only novation transfers obligations; assignment does not impose burdens on the assignee absent consent.
n.2: Assignment typically does not require the debtor’s consent unless restricted; novation requires consent of all parties.
n.3: This inverts the correct position: novation moves both rights and obligations; assignment is rights only.
n.4: Either mechanism may be used, subject to contract terms and consent requirements.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following statements about mirror wills is correct?
o: They are identical wills made by two people, usually spouses, leaving assets to each other
They are joint wills that cannot be changed after the first death
They automatically transfer property to children on death
They revoke all previous wills of both spouses
They are informal oral wills recognised in emergencies
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Mirror wills are two separate wills with similar terms, commonly used by spouses, leaving estates to each other or to the same beneficiaries.

n.1: Joint wills are binding after the first death; mirror wills can be changed independently.
n.2: Mirror wills do not automatically transfer assets to children unless expressly stated.
n.3: All wills revoke earlier wills, but that is not unique to mirror wills.
n.4: Oral wills are only valid in limited military or maritime situations, not typical mirror wills.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: What is the function of a letter of wishes in estate planning?
o: It guides trustees or executors but is not legally binding
It overrides the terms of a will
It creates a binding trust obligation
It replaces the need for a codicil
It must be registered with the Probate Registry
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A letter of wishes provides guidance to trustees or executors on how the testator would like matters handled, but it has no legal force.

n.1: It cannot override the formal provisions of a will.
n.2: It does not impose binding legal obligations.
n.3: Codicils are formal amendments; letters of wishes do not replace them.
n.4: Registration is not required for validity.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: In company liquidation, which party is last in the order of priority for repayment?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Shareholders are residual claimants and only receive payment if all creditors have been satisfied in full.

n.1: Preferential creditors rank above unsecured creditors.
n.2: Fixed charge holders are paid first, not last.
n.3: Unsecured creditors rank above shareholders but below secured creditors.
n.4: Floating charge holders rank above unsecured creditors but below fixed and preferential creditors.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: If a person dies without a valid will and leaves a spouse and children, what happens under intestacy rules?
o: The spouse receives personal chattels, a statutory legacy and a share of the residue
The entire estate passes to the children equally
The entire estate passes to the spouse automatically
The estate is divided equally among spouse, children, and siblings
The Crown immediately inherits the estate
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Under intestacy rules, the spouse receives personal belongings, a statutory legacy, and half the remainder; the children share the other half.

n.1: Children inherit only part of the estate if a spouse survives, not the whole estate.
n.2: The spouse does not automatically inherit the entire estate if children exist.
n.3: Siblings inherit only if there is no surviving spouse or children.
n.4: The Crown inherits only if no surviving relatives fall within intestacy provisions.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which principle governs a minor beneficiary’s inheritance until they reach adulthood?
o: Property is held on statutory trust until age 18
Funds are automatically transferred to guardians
Funds are forfeited until the beneficiary marries
Executors may distribute assets at their discretion
The estate must remain unadministered until adulthood
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Under intestacy, assets for minor beneficiaries are held on statutory trust until they reach 18.

n.1: Guardians may care for minors but do not automatically hold their inheritance.
n.2: Marriage is not a condition of inheritance under intestacy.
n.3: Executors cannot arbitrarily distribute assets; statutory trusts apply.
n.4: Estates are always administered regardless of beneficiary age.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: What is the purpose of the 'prescribed part' in insolvency law?
o: To set aside funds from floating charge realisations for unsecured creditors
To guarantee payment to fixed charge holders
To reimburse directors’ salaries before insolvency
To cover legal costs of administration
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The prescribed part ring-fences part of floating charge realisations for unsecured creditors, improving fairness in distributions.

n.1: Fixed charge holders are paid first in full; the prescribed part does not apply.
n.2: Directors’ salaries are not prioritised by the prescribed part.
n.3: Legal costs are paid but not from the prescribed part fund.
n.4: Shareholders are last in priority and not beneficiaries of the prescribed part.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which type of ownership arises when two or more persons purchase land as tenants in common?
o: Each party owns a distinct share which can pass by will
Each party owns the whole property jointly
Ownership automatically transfers to the survivor
Neither party may transfer their share independently
Ownership is extinguished on death of any party
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Tenants in common each hold a separate, definable share of the property, which may be disposed of by will or sale.

n.1: Joint tenants own the whole collectively; tenants in common own distinct shares.
n.2: Survivorship applies to joint tenancy, not tenancy in common.
n.3: Each party can transfer their share independently, subject to trust rules.
n.4: The deceased’s share is not extinguished; it passes under their estate.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which insolvency term describes continuing to trade to maximise creditor returns after liquidation begins?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Liquidators may allow trading in liquidation if it benefits creditors by maximising the realisation of assets.

n.1: Fraudulent trading involves intent to defraud creditors, not maximising value.
n.2: Wrongful trading relates to directors trading beyond insolvency, not liquidators.
n.3: Administration is a separate insolvency procedure.
n.4: Receivership is enforcement by secured creditors, not trading for all creditors.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which principle ensures that unsecured creditors are treated equally in insolvency?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The pari passu principle requires that unsecured creditors share equally in available assets in proportion to their claims.

n.1: The prescribed part sets aside funds from floating charges, but pari passu governs equal sharing.
n.2: Right of survivorship applies to property co-ownership, not insolvency.
n.3: Privity concerns who can enforce contracts, not creditor equality.
n.4: Promissory estoppel prevents reneging on promises, not insolvency distributions.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: If a person dies intestate, how are their assets distributed?
o: According to statutory rules set out in the Administration of Estates Act
According to the deceased’s oral wishes
Equally among all friends and relatives
Automatically to the Crown, regardless of heirs
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Where no valid will exists, the Administration of Estates Act 1925 sets statutory rules of intestacy to determine asset distribution.

n.1: Oral wishes are not legally binding without a valid will.
n.2: Distribution is not equally among all relatives; there is a fixed statutory order.
n.3: Local authorities do not decide distribution; law governs intestacy.
n.4: The Crown inherits only if no eligible relatives exist under intestacy rules.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following is true about intestacy when a person leaves no spouse, children, parents, or siblings?
o: The estate passes to more distant relatives such as uncles and aunts
The estate is divided among close friends
The estate is transferred to the local authority
The estate passes to any named guardian
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Intestacy rules distribute estates to increasingly distant relatives, such as uncles, aunts, or cousins, before assets go to the Crown.

n.1: Friends are not recognised heirs under intestacy law.
n.2: Local authorities do not inherit under intestacy rules.
n.3: Executors only administer estates, not inherit unless named beneficiaries.
n.4: Guardianship of children does not create inheritance rights.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: What is the effect of divorce on a will in England and Wales?
o: Provisions for the former spouse are treated as if they had died
The entire will is revoked automatically
The will remains unchanged and fully effective
The spouse inherits only personal possessions
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: On divorce, gifts to and appointments of the ex-spouse in a will are treated as if they had predeceased, but the rest of the will remains valid.

n.1: Divorce does not revoke the entire will; marriage does.
n.2: The will is altered only regarding the ex-spouse, not unaffected in general.
n.3: The spouse’s entitlement does not reduce by half; it ceases altogether.
n.4: The spouse does not inherit possessions unless the will specifically leaves them.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which statement best describes consideration in a simple (non-deed) contract for an investment service?
o: Each party must provide something of value in exchange
Only the client must provide consideration
Consideration can be purely past performance
Consideration is unnecessary if terms are in writing
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A simple contract requires reciprocal consideration: the client’s payment/commitment and the firm’s promise to provide services.

n.1: Both sides normally provide consideration; otherwise, the promise may be unenforceable absent a deed.
n.2: Past consideration is not good consideration in English law; it must be bargained for at the time.
n.3: Writing alone does not dispense with consideration unless executed as a deed.
n.4: Regulatory disclosures are compliance obligations, not bargained-for consideration.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which creditor group is paid after preferential creditors but before unsecured creditors?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Floating charge holders are paid after preferential creditors, subject to the prescribed part for unsecured creditors.

n.1: Fixed charge holders are paid first, before preferential creditors.
n.2: Trade creditors are unsecured and rank lower.
n.3: Shareholders are residual claimants and paid last.
n.4: Directors are not a creditor class by default; they may rank as unsecured if owed money.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following correctly describes a trust deed?
o: It is the formal legal document establishing the terms of a trust
It is a probate document granting executors authority
It is a statutory intestacy form
It is a codicil amending a will
It is an agreement between trustees and beneficiaries only
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A trust deed is the legal instrument creating and governing a trust, setting out trustee powers and beneficiary rights.

n.1: A grant of probate, not a trust deed, gives executors authority.
n.2: Intestacy is governed by statute, not by a deed.
n.3: A codicil amends a will, not a trust.
n.4: Trust deeds involve settlors, trustees, and beneficiaries, not just trustees and beneficiaries.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which principle governs situations where one party relies on another’s promise without formal consideration?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Promissory estoppel prevents a party from going back on a promise when the other party has reasonably relied upon it, even without consideration.

n.1: Ratification involves approving an agent’s unauthorised acts, not promises without consideration.
n.2: Frustration concerns supervening impossibility, not reliance on promises.
n.3: Privity determines who may enforce contracts, not enforceability of gratuitous promises.
n.4: Agency by estoppel arises from representations of authority, not contract promises.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which rule governs when acceptance takes effect under the ‘postal rule’?
o: Acceptance is effective when posted, not when received
Acceptance is effective when received by the offeror
Acceptance is effective when read by the offeror
Acceptance is effective only if acknowledged
Acceptance is effective only once consideration is provided
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The postal rule provides that acceptance is effective when properly posted, even if it is delayed or lost, unless excluded.

n.1: This applies to instantaneous communications, not the postal rule.
n.2: Physical reading by the offeror is not required for acceptance under the postal rule.
n.3: Acknowledgement is not generally required for postal acceptance.
n.4: Consideration is a separate requirement, not the trigger for acceptance.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which situation would most likely give rise to a constructive trust?
o: Property acquired by one party but held for another due to fairness
Two parties signing a deed of trust
A settlor formally transferring assets into a trust
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Constructive trusts are imposed by courts to address unfairness, such as property acquired in circumstances where it is inequitable for one party to retain sole benefit.

n.1: A deed of trust creates an express trust, not a constructive one.
n.2: A settlor creating a trust is a formal express trust, not constructive.
n.3: Executors distribute assets under wills, not constructive trusts.
n.4: Dividends are contractual rights under company law, not trusts.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: What happens if a residuary beneficiary in a will dies before the testator?
o: The gift usually lapses unless substituted beneficiaries are named
The gift passes automatically to the executor
The gift is redirected to the Crown
The gift must be divided equally between all remaining relatives
The gift is held in trust until reassigned by the court
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: If a residuary beneficiary predeceases the testator, their gift lapses unless the will names a substitute or statutory anti-lapse rules apply.

n.1: Executors do not inherit unless also named beneficiaries.
n.2: The Crown inherits only when no heirs exist.
n.3: Estate division follows the will or intestacy, not arbitrary equal shares.
n.4: Courts do not automatically create trusts for lapsed gifts unless directed.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which remedy aims to restore parties to their pre-contractual position?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Rescission unwinds a contract, attempting to return both parties to the position before it was made.

n.1: Specific performance compels performance, not reversal.
n.2: Damages compensate loss, not restore pre-contract position.
n.3: Rectification corrects written errors, not restores parties to pre-contract state.
n.4: Injunctions prevent actions but do not unwind contracts.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which rule applies if a beneficiary dies within 28 days of the testator?
o: The rule in Saunders v Vautier
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The survivorship rule requires beneficiaries to survive the testator by 28 days unless the will provides otherwise, or the gift lapses.

n.1: Intestacy applies only if there is no valid will or gift.
n.2: Per stirpes governs distribution among descendants, not survivorship periods.
n.3: Saunders v Vautier allows beneficiaries to demand trust termination, unrelated to survivorship.
n.4: Anti-lapse provisions apply to certain relatives, but survivorship rules still operate.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which statutory procedure allows companies to reach a binding compromise with creditors to avoid liquidation?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A CVA allows a company to reach an agreement with its creditors, supervised by an insolvency practitioner, to repay debts over time while avoiding liquidation.

n.1: Administration may lead to restructuring but is not primarily a compromise procedure.
n.2: Receivership involves secured creditors enforcing their rights, not compromise with all creditors.
n.3: Debt Relief Orders apply to individuals, not companies.
n.4: Bankruptcy is an individual process, not a corporate one.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which trust ensures income for a surviving spouse while preserving capital for children?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Life interest trusts give a beneficiary, often a spouse, the right to income for life, while preserving the capital for others, often children.

n.1: Discretionary trusts give trustees flexibility, not fixed life income rights.
n.2: Protective trusts restrict access on bankruptcy, not preserve capital for heirs.
n.3: Bare trusts give absolute entitlement, not life income rights.
n.4: Constructive trusts are imposed by courts, not created for succession planning.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which insolvency officer is appointed to manage an individual’s estate during bankruptcy?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The trustee in bankruptcy takes control of the bankrupt’s assets, realises them, and distributes funds to creditors.

n.1: Liquidators deal with companies, not individuals.
n.2: Company secretaries manage corporate administration, not personal insolvency.
n.3: Court registrars handle filings but do not manage bankrupt estates.
n.4: Advisers may guide debtors but are not appointed officers of the court.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following is a requirement for a valid will under English law?
o: It must be in writing, signed and witnessed by two people
It must be handwritten by the testator
It must be registered with the Probate Registry
It must be signed by three witnesses
It must be notarised by a solicitor
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A valid will must be in writing, signed by the testator, and witnessed by two independent witnesses under the Wills Act 1837.

n.1: There is no requirement for a will to be handwritten; it may be typed.
n.2: Registration is not mandatory in England and Wales; a will is valid without it.
n.3: Only two witnesses are required, not three.
n.4: Notarisation is not required; witnessing by two individuals is sufficient.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: What is the main purpose of administration as a corporate insolvency procedure?
o: To protect the company from creditor action while restructuring
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Administration provides breathing space from creditor enforcement to attempt a rescue or restructuring of the company.

n.1: Dissolution is the outcome of liquidation, not administration.
n.2: Creditors, not shareholders, are prioritised in insolvency.
n.3: Directors may be displaced during administration but not always permanently.
n.4: Administration focuses on the company’s assets, not enforcing personal guarantees.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which doctrine prevents property from passing under intestacy if the deceased unlawfully caused the death of the heir?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The forfeiture rule prevents a person who unlawfully killed the deceased from inheriting under a will or intestacy.

n.1: Pari passu applies to insolvency distributions, not succession.
n.2: Consideration is a contract principle, not inheritance law.
n.3: Lapse applies when beneficiaries predecease the testator, not unlawful killing.
n.4: Survivorship ensures property passes to survivors, not exclusions due to crime.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which document is typically required to administer a deceased’s estate under a valid will?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A grant of probate is issued by the court confirming an executor’s authority to administer the estate.

n.1: A trust deed creates or governs trusts, not probate.
n.2: Codicils amend wills but are not probate authority.
n.3: Deed polls change names, not administer estates.
n.4: Letters of wishes guide trustees but are not legally binding probate documents.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which best describes a bare trust in investment holdings?
o: Trustees hold legal title but act only on beneficiaries’ instructions
Trustees actively manage assets with full discretion
Beneficiaries have no enforceable rights against trustees
Trustees acquire beneficial ownership alongside legal title
The trust itself owns the assets as a legal entity
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: In a bare trust, trustees hold legal title but must act on directions of beneficiaries, who hold the entire beneficial interest.

n.1: Discretionary trusts give trustees powers to manage assets, not bare trusts.
n.2: Beneficiaries of a bare trust do have enforceable equitable rights.
n.3: Trustees in a bare trust hold legal title only, not beneficial ownership.
n.4: A trust is not itself a separate legal entity; trustees own assets for beneficiaries.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following best explains why trustees owe fiduciary duties?
o: Because they must act solely in the best interests of beneficiaries
Because they are personally entitled to trust property
Because they inherit property under intestacy rules
Because they are automatically executors of wills
Because they guarantee financial returns to beneficiaries
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Trustees are fiduciaries and must act in good faith, avoid conflicts of interest, and act solely in the beneficiaries’ best interests.

n.1: Trustees hold legal title but not beneficial entitlement.
n.2: Intestacy distributes property via statutory rules, not trusteeship.
n.3: Executors may also be trustees, but the roles are separate.
n.4: Trustees must act prudently but cannot guarantee returns.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which statement best explains why a company is considered a legal person?
o: It has separate legal personality distinct from its members
It is owned collectively by its shareholders
It is managed by directors on behalf of shareholders
It can only contract through employees
It is recognised as part of the partnership
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A company has separate legal personality under the Companies Act, enabling it to contract, sue, and own property in its own name.

n.1: Shareholders own shares, not the company’s assets; the company is distinct from its members.
n.2: Management by directors does not define legal personality; it is a statutory consequence of incorporation.
n.3: Companies can contract through various agents, not only employees.
n.4: Companies are not partnerships; they are separate legal persons.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which situation demonstrates undue influence in contract law?
o: A vulnerable client pressured by an adviser into signing an unsuitable agreement
A client agreeing to terms without reading them
An agent exceeding actual authority but within apparent authority
A mistake about contract subject matter by both parties
A contract discharged due to impossibility of performance
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Undue influence arises when one party exploits a position of trust or pressure to secure a contract, often rendering it voidable.

n.1: Failing to read terms is not undue influence, though it may affect understanding.
n.2: This concerns agency authority, not undue influence.
n.3: Mistake is a separate doctrine, not undue influence.
n.4: Frustration discharges contracts but is unrelated to undue influence.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which type of ownership applies when shares are held in the name of a nominee company for the benefit of an investor?
o: Legal title with nominee, beneficial interest with investor
Legal title and beneficial interest with nominee
Beneficial interest with nominee, legal title with investor
Both legal and beneficial title with custodian
Joint tenancy between nominee and investor
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: In nominee arrangements, the nominee holds legal title, but the beneficial interest remains with the underlying investor.

n.1: Nominees do not take beneficial interest; they act as bare trustees.
n.2: The investor does not hold legal title once transferred to the nominee.
n.3: Custodians generally hold legal, not beneficial, title.
n.4: Nominee arrangements are not co-ownership; there is no joint tenancy.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which principle is most relevant when a person without authority acts and the principal later refuses to accept the contract?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: If the principal refuses to ratify, the contract remains unauthorised and does not bind the principal.

n.1: Promissory estoppel prevents going back on promises, not refusal to ratify.
n.2: Consideration relates to enforceability, not ratification.
n.3: Survivorship is a property concept, not agency law.
n.4: Privity restricts enforcement to contract parties, not ratification issues.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following assets usually passes outside of a will or intestacy?
o: Jointly owned property passing by survivorship
Cash savings in sole bank accounts
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Jointly owned property held as joint tenants passes automatically to the survivor, outside the will or intestacy process.

n.1: Personal jewellery owned solely by the deceased passes under the will or intestacy.
n.2: Private company shares form part of the estate unless held jointly.
n.3: Sole bank accounts are estate assets subject to will or intestacy.
n.4: Individually owned property passes through the estate.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which document typically evidences ownership of shares in a company?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A share certificate is issued to a shareholder as evidence of legal title to shares in the company.

n.1: A prospectus offers securities to the public but does not evidence ownership.
n.2: The memorandum sets out company objectives, not ownership of shares.
n.3: Annual reports provide financial information but do not prove ownership.
n.4: Articles outline governance rules, not evidence of ownership.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which situation demonstrates ratification in the law of agency?
o: A principal later approves a contract made without authority by an agent
An agent acts within scope of actual authority granted
A client signs a contract directly with the provider
A firm dismisses an agent for misconduct
A contract is void due to lack of consideration
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Ratification occurs when a principal retrospectively approves an act done on their behalf but without prior authority.

n.1: Acts within actual authority need no ratification.
n.2: Direct contracts do not involve agency principles requiring ratification.
n.3: Dismissal of an agent is unrelated to ratification.
n.4: Consideration relates to validity of contracts, not agency ratification.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which insolvency procedure is commonly used by secured lenders to recover money from assets subject to a floating charge?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Administrative receivership allows a floating charge holder to appoint a receiver to realise company assets and repay debts.

n.1: Compulsory liquidation winds up a company but is not initiated by secured lenders.
n.2: Debt Relief Orders apply only to individuals with low debts.
n.3: IVAs are arrangements for individuals, not secured lenders.
n.4: Bankruptcy applies to individuals, not companies.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which statement best defines a power of attorney?
o: A legal document authorising another to act on behalf of the donor
A statutory right for advisers to manage client assets
A court order compelling third parties to act
A beneficial interest in property transferred to an agent
A deed transferring full ownership to a representative
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A power of attorney is a legal instrument where a donor appoints an attorney to act on their behalf in specified matters.

n.1: Advisers require regulatory authorisation, not a statutory right under a power of attorney.
n.2: A power of attorney is a private arrangement, not a court order.
n.3: An attorney does not obtain beneficial ownership of assets.
n.4: A power of attorney grants authority to act, not ownership transfer.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Under English law, which contract is unenforceable due to lack of capacity?
o: A minor signing a long-term credit agreement
An adult signing a tenancy agreement
A company contracting with a supplier
A partnership contracting with a bank
A trustee purchasing investments for a trust
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Minors generally lack capacity for binding contracts, except for necessities or beneficial contracts of service.

n.1: An adult generally has full capacity unless restricted by mental incapacity.
n.2: Companies are separate legal persons capable of contracting.
n.3: Partnerships can enter into contracts in their business name.
n.4: Trustees have authority to contract when acting within their powers.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which feature of a company limited by shares protects its shareholders?
o: Limited liability up to the value of unpaid shares
Full legal title to company assets
Protection against insolvency of the company
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Shareholders’ liability is limited to any unpaid amounts on their shares, protecting personal assets from company debts.

n.1: Dividends are not guaranteed; they depend on profits and board decisions.
n.2: Company assets belong to the company, not shareholders directly.
n.3: Management authority lies with directors, not shareholders (unless acting collectively).
n.4: Shareholders are not shielded from insolvency; they may lose their investment.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which statutory offence occurs if a director deliberately conceals company assets during insolvency?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Fraudulent trading includes intentionally concealing assets to defraud creditors, which can attract criminal penalties.

n.1: Wrongful trading is trading past insolvency without intent to defraud.
n.2: Breach of fiduciary duty relates to duties owed by directors generally, not concealment.
n.3: Negligence is failure of care, not deliberate concealment.
n.4: Misrepresentation involves false statements, not hiding assets.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which requirement must be satisfied before a Lasting Power of Attorney (Property and Financial Affairs) can be used by the attorney?
o: It must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian
It must be witnessed by a solicitor and a doctor
It only takes effect after the donor loses capacity
It must be re-executed every five years
It must be lodged at the Court of Protection before first use
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: An LPA must be registered with the OPG before the attorney can act. A Property and Financial Affairs LPA can, if the donor wishes, be used while the donor still has capacity.

n.1: Specific witnessing by a solicitor and a doctor is not a general requirement; a certificate provider and witnesses suffice per prescribed form.
n.2: This LPA can be used before loss of capacity if the donor has not restricted it.
n.3: There is no automatic re-execution cycle; an LPA endures until revoked or the donor dies.
n.4: Lodging at the Court of Protection is not routinely required for use; registration with the OPG is.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following is the main role of an executor named in a will?
o: To administer the estate and distribute assets according to the will
To act as a beneficiary of the estate
To provide legal advice to the family
To alter the will if circumstances change
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Executors are appointed to carry out the instructions of the will, administer the estate, and distribute assets accordingly.

n.1: An executor may also be a beneficiary, but their primary duty is administration.
n.2: Executors are not required to provide legal advice; they act in a fiduciary role.
n.3: Executors cannot choose beneficiaries; they must follow the will.
n.4: Executors cannot unilaterally alter a will; variations require agreement of beneficiaries.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which type of power of attorney automatically ceases if the donor loses mental capacity?
o: General power of attorney registered with the OPG
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: An ordinary power of attorney is valid only while the donor has capacity; it automatically ends if capacity is lost.

n.1: A Lasting Power of Attorney continues even after capacity is lost, once registered.
n.2: Enduring powers, though now replaced, also survive loss of capacity if registered.
n.3: Registration with the OPG does not prevent an ordinary POA from ceasing at incapacity.
n.4: A deed of trust is not a power of attorney and does not grant authority to act for another.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which authority allows an attorney under a Property and Financial Affairs LPA to manage investments?
o: Specific powers included in the registered LPA document
The FCA’s statutory rules on conduct of business
The adviser’s appointment letter from the firm
The donor’s oral instructions to the attorney
A general assumption of authority in financial services
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Attorneys can only act within the express powers granted in the registered LPA document for property and financial matters.

n.1: FCA rules govern authorised firms, not attorneys acting for individuals.
n.2: An adviser’s appointment letter has no effect on the attorney’s legal powers.
n.3: Oral instructions cannot override or extend the written authority in the LPA.
n.4: Authority must be expressly documented; it cannot be assumed.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which statute governs intestacy rules in England and Wales?
o: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The Administration of Estates Act 1925 sets out intestacy rules in England and Wales, determining how estates are distributed without a will.

n.1: The Trustee Act 2000 modernises trustee powers but does not govern intestacy.
n.2: The Inheritance Act 1975 allows family members to claim provision, but intestacy is governed by the 1925 Act.
n.3: The Law of Property Act governs property rights, not intestacy.
n.4: The Succession Act 1965 applies in Ireland, not England and Wales.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which insolvency process provides relief for sole traders similar to bankruptcy?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Sole traders are individuals, so bankruptcy is the equivalent process, allowing debts to be written off and assets realised.

n.1: CVAs apply to companies, not sole traders.
n.2: Administration is corporate, not individual.
n.3: Liquidation applies to companies.
n.4: Receivership relates to secured lending against company assets.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: What is the effect of the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975?
o: It allows certain dependants to claim reasonable financial provision from an estate
It prevents gifts to foreign beneficiaries
It ensures children always inherit equally
It sets the statutory intestacy order
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The Act allows dependants to claim reasonable financial provision if a will or intestacy does not provide adequately for them.

n.1: Divorce may affect wills, but this Act specifically concerns financial provision.
n.2: The Act does not prohibit gifts to overseas beneficiaries.
n.3: Children do not always inherit equally; distribution depends on wills or intestacy.
n.4: The intestacy order is set by the Administration of Estates Act 1925.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which insolvency outcome occurs if an Individual Voluntary Arrangement fails?
o: The debtor may face bankruptcy proceedings
The IVA is automatically extended for five years
The debtor is released from all debts
The court annuls all creditor claims
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: If an IVA fails, creditors may petition for the debtor’s bankruptcy to recover debts through asset realisation.

n.1: An IVA does not extend automatically if it fails.
n.2: Failure does not release the debtor; debts remain.
n.3: Creditors are not bound indefinitely if the arrangement fails.
n.4: Creditors’ claims remain valid; they are not annulled.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following is required for a valid holographic will?
o: It must be entirely handwritten and signed by the testator
It must be typed and witnessed by two solicitors
It must be sealed and notarised
It must be registered with the Probate Registry
It must be written jointly by spouses
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A holographic will is one written entirely by hand and signed by the testator, though still subject to local legal recognition rules.

n.1: Typed wills are valid if properly signed and witnessed, but are not holographic.
n.2: Sealing and notarisation are not standard requirements.
n.3: Registration is not necessary for validity in England and Wales.
n.4: Joint wills are separate instruments, not holographic.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following best defines a protective trust?
o: A trust that restricts beneficiaries’ access if they become bankrupt
A trust that gives beneficiaries fixed income for life
A trust created by court order only
A bare trust with immediate entitlement
A trust that trustees must dissolve within 10 years
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A protective trust provides income to a beneficiary but converts into a discretionary trust if the beneficiary becomes bankrupt or attempts to assign their interest.

n.1: Fixed income is characteristic of interest in possession trusts, not protective trusts.
n.2: Protective trusts can be created by settlors, not just courts.
n.3: Bare trusts confer full entitlement, not restrictions.
n.4: Trusts do not have a statutory 10-year dissolution requirement.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which insolvency role is appointed to oversee repayment under an Individual Voluntary Arrangement?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: An insolvency practitioner supervises IVAs, ensuring debtor repayments are distributed to creditors according to agreed terms.

n.1: The Official Receiver administers bankruptcies, not IVAs.
n.2: Directors may initiate arrangements but cannot supervise IVAs.
n.3: Courts approve IVAs but do not supervise repayments.
n.4: Advisers may explain options but cannot formally supervise IVAs.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which statute governs trustee powers and duties in England and Wales?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The Trustee Act 2000 modernised trustee powers, including investment duties and delegation of functions.

n.1: The Wills Act governs formalities of wills, not trustee powers.
n.2: The Law of Property Act covers property rights generally, not trusteeship.
n.3: The Inheritance Act allows claims for provision, not trustee duties.
n.4: The Companies Act governs corporate law, not trusts.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which party typically holds legal title in a unit trust structure?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: In a unit trust, trustees hold legal title to the assets on behalf of unit holders, who have the beneficial interest.

n.1: Investors hold the beneficial, not legal, interest.
n.2: The manager directs investments but does not hold legal title.
n.3: The FCA regulates funds but does not hold title to assets.
n.4: Beneficial owners have equitable rights, not legal title.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which debt is excluded from discharge in bankruptcy due to public policy?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Debts obtained by fraud or dishonesty are excluded from discharge, ensuring misconduct is not rewarded by bankruptcy protection.

n.1: Bank loans are dischargeable in bankruptcy.
n.2: Credit card debts are normally discharged.
n.3: Utility arrears are unsecured debts and dischargeable.
n.4: Medical bills are dischargeable unless fraud is involved.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which body oversees the regulation of insolvency practitioners in the UK?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Insolvency practitioners are authorised and regulated by Recognised Professional Bodies such as ICAEW and IPA, under oversight of the Insolvency Service.

n.1: The FCA regulates financial services, not insolvency practitioners.
n.2: The PRA supervises banks and insurers, not insolvency practitioners.
n.3: Companies House registers filings but does not regulate practitioners.
n.4: The CMA focuses on competition and consumer law, not insolvency.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Two spouses hold their home as joint tenants. Which feature applies on one spouse’s death?
o: The survivor automatically owns the whole by survivorship
The deceased’s share passes under their will
Each owns a fixed proportion that can be sold separately
The title converts into tenants in common by default
The property must be sold to realise the deceased’s share
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Joint tenancy features the right of survivorship: the deceased’s interest extinguishes and the survivor takes the whole.

n.1: Under a joint tenancy the interest does not pass via will or intestacy; it passes by survivorship.
n.2: Fixed shares are a feature of tenants in common, not joint tenants.
n.3: Conversion requires severance by notice or act; it is not automatic on death.
n.4: A sale is not mandated by law merely due to the death of a joint tenant.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following is an example of a demonstrative legacy?
o: £5,000 to be paid from a named bank account
A gold ring to a niece
Half the residue of the estate to a spouse
A property gifted to a child
All personal chattels to a brother
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A demonstrative legacy is a gift of money payable from a specific source, such as a named bank account or investment fund.

n.1: A gold ring is a specific legacy, not demonstrative.
n.2: A share of the residue is a residuary legacy.
n.3: A property gift is a specific devise, not demonstrative.
n.4: Personal chattels are specific legacies, not demonstrative legacies.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which insolvency process is designed to maximise returns to creditors while giving viable companies a chance to survive?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Administration protects companies from enforcement while a strategy is pursued to rescue or maximise creditor returns.

n.1: Liquidation focuses on dissolving the company, not survival.
n.2: Receivership benefits the appointing creditor, not all creditors collectively.
n.3: Debt Relief Orders are for individuals with small debts.
n.4: Bankruptcy applies to individuals, not companies.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following is an equitable remedy for breach of contract?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Specific performance is an equitable remedy compelling a party to perform contractual obligations rather than pay damages.

n.1: Damages are a common law remedy, not equitable.
n.2: Penalty clauses are unenforceable; courts may strike them out.
n.3: Liquidated damages are contractual terms, not equitable remedies.
n.4: Termination is a common law remedy, not equitable relief.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which intestacy rule applies if a person dies leaving no relatives?
o: The estate passes to the Crown as bona vacantia
The estate is retained by the probate registry
The estate is redistributed to local charities
The estate is passed to the Insolvency Service
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: If no relatives are entitled under intestacy, the estate passes to the Crown as bona vacantia.

n.1: The probate registry does not retain estates.
n.2: Charities may benefit if named in wills, but not under intestacy.
n.3: The Insolvency Service does not handle intestacy estates.
n.4: The estate is always administered; it cannot remain ownerless.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which principle allows creditors to offset mutual debts during insolvency proceedings?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Insolvency set-off requires mutual debts between the insolvent and creditors to be offset, with only the balance claimable in proceedings.

n.1: Pari passu governs equal treatment, not set-off.
n.2: Privity governs who can enforce contracts, not set-off.
n.3: Consideration concerns contract formation, not insolvency set-off.
n.4: Estoppel prevents denial of promises, not set-off in insolvency.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which statutory requirement must be met for trustees when investing trust funds?
o: They must have regard to the standard investment criteria
They must guarantee a minimum return to beneficiaries
They must invest only in government bonds
They must seek approval from beneficiaries for all decisions
They must hold all assets in cash
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Under the Trustee Act 2000, trustees must have regard to the standard investment criteria, including suitability and diversification.

n.1: Trustees cannot guarantee returns; they must act prudently.
n.2: Trustees are not restricted to government bonds.
n.3: Beneficiary consent is not needed for routine investment decisions.
n.4: Holding all assets in cash would usually breach the duty to diversify.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: When a bank provides a mortgage loan, what interest does it usually hold in the property?
o: Full legal title to the property
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The bank typically takes a legal charge over the property, securing repayment of the mortgage without owning the property outright.

n.1: The bank does not hold beneficial ownership; the borrower retains it.
n.2: The bank does not acquire legal title unless repossession occurs after default.
n.3: A tenancy in common is co-ownership, not a lender’s security interest.
n.4: Nominee arrangements relate to investment custody, not mortgages.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which element of a valid contract ensures both parties intend their agreement to be legally enforceable?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: For a contract to be enforceable, the parties must intend that their agreement will create legal obligations.

n.1: Consideration is needed for simple contracts, but it is not intention to create legal relations.
n.2: An offer is necessary, but without intention the agreement may be social or domestic in nature.
n.3: Acceptance is key to agreement, but not sufficient to show intention.
n.4: Capacity ensures parties can contract, but does not prove intention to be bound.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Under agency principles relevant to retail investment business, an appointed representative’s acts are treated in law as whose acts?
o: The authorised firm that is the principal
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The AR acts as agent of the authorised principal firm, which bears responsibility to clients for regulated activities within the scope of appointment.

n.1: Liability typically attaches to the principal rather than resting solely on the AR.
n.2: A product provider is not the principal unless expressly appointing and assuming responsibility.
n.3: Compliance officers supervise but are not the legal principal in client contracts.
n.4: FOS is a dispute-resolution body, not a contracting principal.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: What is the typical discharge period for bankruptcy in England and Wales?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Most bankrupts are automatically discharged after 12 months, although restrictions may continue longer in serious cases.

n.1: 6 months is too short; the statutory discharge is usually 12 months.
n.2: 24 months is longer than the typical period.
n.3: 36 months applies to certain repayment plans, not standard discharge.
n.4: 5 years is not the statutory period; discharge normally occurs after one year.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: What is the maximum period for which a bankruptcy restrictions order can extend restrictions on a bankrupt?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: A bankruptcy restrictions order can extend restrictions for up to 15 years in cases of misconduct.

n.1: 3 years is too short; repayment orders may last this long, but BROs can be much longer.
n.2: 5 years is possible but not the statutory maximum.
n.3: 7 years is within the range, but the maximum is 15.
n.4: 10 years may be imposed but is not the maximum limit.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which factor distinguishes real property from personal property?
o: Real property is immovable land or interests in land
Real property consists of moveable goods
Personal property always requires a deed to transfer
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Real property refers to land and interests attached to land, whereas personal property includes movable and intangible assets.

n.1: Moveable goods are personal property, not real property.
n.2: Personal property is transferable unless legally restricted.
n.3: Many personal property transfers do not require a deed.
n.4: Bank deposits are personal property, not real property.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which official handles initial bankruptcy cases if no insolvency practitioner is appointed?
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: The Official Receiver, a civil servant, initially administers bankruptcies and liquidations before an insolvency practitioner may be appointed.

n.1: Judges make bankruptcy orders but do not manage estates.
n.2: Directors may apply for liquidation but cannot manage bankruptcy estates.
n.3: Advisers can guide clients but have no formal role in bankruptcy administration.
n.4: The Treasury Solicitor is not responsible for insolvency estates.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which legal principle is engaged if a client contract is void due to illegal purpose?
o: Illegality renders the contract void ab initio
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Contracts formed for an illegal purpose are void ab initio, meaning they never had legal effect.

n.1: Misrepresentation makes a contract voidable, not automatically void.
n.2: Frustration arises from supervening events, not illegality at inception.
n.3: Undue influence deals with improper pressure, not illegality.
n.4: Mistake can void contracts, but illegality specifically voids them from the start.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Under the Insolvency Act 1986, which of the following best describes bankruptcy?
o: A court order made against an individual who cannot pay their debts
A voluntary arrangement agreed by a company’s creditors
The compulsory winding up of a limited company
An informal agreement between a debtor and creditors
A debt management plan approved by the FCA
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: Bankruptcy under the Insolvency Act 1986 is a court-based process for individuals unable to meet debt obligations, with assets realised to repay creditors.

n.1: A voluntary arrangement is separate from bankruptcy and may prevent it.
n.2: Compulsory winding up applies to companies, not individuals.
n.3: Informal agreements are outside the formal insolvency framework.
n.4: Debt management plans are informal and regulated by the FCA, not court bankruptcy orders.

Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.q: Which of the following most accurately describes an enduring power of attorney (EPA)?
o: It remains valid if the donor loses mental capacity, provided it is registered
It is identical to an ordinary power of attorney
It can only be used for health and welfare decisions
It must be re-executed every three years
It is automatically invalid after the donor’s death
Financial Advice Legal Concepts & Consid.w: EPAs, created before their replacement by LPAs, continue after incapacity if registered with the OPG.

n.1: Ordinary powers end with incapacity; EPAs survive it.
n.2: EPAs are for property and financial affairs, not health and welfare.
