n.2: The MPC focuses on inflation and interest rates, not systemic risk management.
n.3: The Risk and Audit Committee oversees internal Bank controls, not macroprudential action.
n.4: The Supervisory Risk Board is not a Bank of England committee with statutory authority.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which body regulates solicitors’ professional conduct in England and Wales?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The Solicitors Regulation Authority regulates solicitors in England and Wales, ensuring high professional standards.

n.1: The Bar Standards Board regulates barristers, not solicitors.
n.2: The FCA regulates financial conduct, not the legal profession.
n.3: The CMA enforces competition law, not solicitor conduct.
n.4: The PRA regulates prudential risks, not solicitors.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which body provides independent dispute resolution for pensions complaints?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The Pensions Ombudsman investigates and resolves complaints about pensions administration and decisions made by pension trustees.

n.1: The FOS handles consumer disputes but not occupational pensions cases, which go to the Pensions Ombudsman.
n.2: The Pensions Regulator oversees schemes but does not resolve disputes.
n.3: The FRC handles reporting and governance, not pension complaints.
n.4: The Bank of England does not resolve pension disputes.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which directive harmonises bank capital requirements within the EU?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The Capital Requirements Directive implements Basel standards in EU law, harmonising capital adequacy across member states.

n.1: Solvency II applies to insurers, not banks.
n.2: UCITS covers investment funds, not bank capital.
n.3: MiFID II regulates investment firm conduct, not capital.
n.4: GDPR regulates data, not bank capital requirements.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which EU directive sets rules for insurance regulation and solvency?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The Solvency II Directive establishes harmonised rules for insurance regulation across the EU, focusing on solvency, capital, and risk management.

n.1: MiFID II regulates financial markets and investor protection, not insurance solvency.
n.2: UCITS governs investment funds, not insurers.
n.3: BRRD concerns failing banks, not insurers.
n.4: PSD regulates payments, not insurance solvency.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which regulation introduced uniform rules for EU financial benchmarks?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The EU Benchmarks Regulation created standards for benchmark administrators to enhance transparency and reduce manipulation risks.

n.1: MiFID II regulates markets, not benchmarks directly.
n.2: UCITS covers funds, not financial benchmarks.
n.3: PSD2 governs payments, not benchmarks.
n.4: Solvency II applies to insurers, not benchmarks.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which body enforces UK advertising standards in broadcast media?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: Ofcom regulates broadcast media and enforces advertising standards alongside the ASA, ensuring compliance in TV and radio advertising.

n.0: The ASA covers non-broadcast advertising, but Ofcom has jurisdiction over broadcast media.
n.1: The FCA regulates financial promotions but not general broadcast advertising standards.
n.3: The Bank manages monetary and financial stability, not advertising.
n.4: The CMA enforces competition, not broadcast advertising.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which directive created harmonised standards for bank recovery and resolution in the EU?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The BRRD sets harmonised EU standards for bank recovery and resolution, ensuring consistency in managing failing banks.

n.1: MiFID II regulates market conduct, not bank resolution.
n.2: UCITS applies to funds, not banks.
n.3: PSD regulates payments, not resolution plans.
n.4: GDPR governs data protection, not bank resolution.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: What is the PRA’s secondary competition objective?
o: Facilitate effective competition in the interests of consumers
Oversee fair trading in securities markets
Set competitive benchmarks for LIBOR alternatives
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The PRA’s secondary competition objective requires it to act, when possible, in ways that facilitate effective competition in the interests of consumers.

n.1: The PRA does not focus on shareholder returns; its remit is prudential safety.
n.2: Listing fees are FCA market conduct matters, not PRA prudential objectives.
n.3: Fair trading in securities is part of FCA’s market integrity role.
n.4: Benchmark setting is not the PRA’s competition role.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: How does HM Treasury exercise control over financial regulation during systemic crises?
o: Provide direction powers over the Bank of England and regulators
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: During systemic crises, HM Treasury may exercise direction powers to instruct the Bank of England or regulators, particularly concerning public funds or resolution tools.

n.1: Redress schemes are established under FCA or FSCS frameworks, not directly by Treasury in crises.
n.2: Routine enforcement remains regulator-led; Treasury directions apply to systemic events.
n.3: Capital plans are prudential regulator decisions, not Treasury’s role.
n.4: Listing suspensions are managed by the FCA, not Treasury powers.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which international standards guide insurers’ solvency and risk management?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS) issues Insurance Core Principles, providing global standards for insurer solvency and risk management.

n.1: Basel III applies to banks, not insurers.
n.2: MiFID II regulates investment firms, not insurers.
n.3: OECD principles relate to governance, not solvency.
n.4: UCITS applies to funds, not insurers.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which UK body enforces data protection laws relevant to financial firms?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The Information Commissioner’s Office enforces UK data protection laws, including GDPR and the Data Protection Act, across all sectors including financial services.

n.1: The FCA focuses on conduct but does not enforce data protection laws.
n.2: The Bank of England manages stability, not data protection.
n.3: The PRA supervises prudential safety, not data protection.
n.4: HM Treasury sets policy but does not enforce data laws.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which Bank of England committee’s decisions directly affect consumer mortgage rates?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The Monetary Policy Committee’s decisions on the base rate directly influence borrowing costs, including mortgage rates for consumers.

n.1: The FPC manages systemic risks, not interest rates affecting mortgages.
n.2: The PRC focuses on prudential policy, not interest rates.
n.3: The Court oversees Bank governance, not mortgage rates.
n.4: The Resolution Directorate deals with failing firms, not consumer interest rates.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which global agreement set minimum standards for bank capital and liquidity?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: Basel III sets global standards on bank capital, liquidity, and leverage, implemented through regional directives such as CRD IV in the EU.

n.1: MiFID II covers investor protection, not bank capital.
n.2: Solvency II applies to insurers, not banks.
n.3: UCITS applies to funds, not bank capital.
n.4: PRIIPs focuses on disclosure for retail investors, not bank capital.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which regulator oversees UK competition in insurance pricing practices?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The CMA enforces competition law across sectors, including investigations into anti-competitive pricing practices in insurance.

n.1: The FCA regulates conduct and consumer outcomes, but competition enforcement sits with the CMA.
n.2: The PRA ensures prudential safety, not competition enforcement.
n.3: The Bank oversees stability, not pricing competition.
n.4: The FOS resolves disputes, not competition issues.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which UK legislation formally established the Financial Policy Committee?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The Financial Services Act 2012 established the FPC within the Bank of England, tasked with macroprudential oversight.

n.1: The Banking Act 2009 created resolution powers, not the FPC.
n.2: FSMA 2000 underpins regulation but did not create the FPC.
n.3: The Companies Act covers corporate law, not central banking.
n.4: The Enterprise Act addresses competition and insolvency, not financial stability.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Where do the threshold conditions sit for authorisation and ongoing permission under FSMA?
o: In statute, with PRA and FCA each applying their own conditions
Only in the FCA Handbook SUP sourcebook
Only in the PRA Rulebook for all firms
In the Listing Rules for premium issuers
In the Bank of England Act as secondary legislation
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: Threshold conditions are set in FSMA and secondary legislation, with distinct conditions applied by the PRA and FCA according to their remits (prudential vs conduct) for authorisation and supervision.

n.1: They are not solely a Handbook procedural matter; they are grounded in statute.
n.2: The PRA does not hold all conditions for all firms; the FCA has its own where relevant.
n.3: Listing Rules address issuers’ market requirements, not FSMA threshold conditions.
n.4: The Bank of England Act is not the home of FSMA threshold conditions.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which regulator ensures compliance with UK data protection law in financial services?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The Information Commissioner’s Office enforces data protection and privacy law across all sectors, including financial services.

n.1: The FCA regulates conduct but not data protection law.
n.2: The Bank focuses on stability, not data law enforcement.
n.3: The PRA supervises prudential risks, not privacy.
n.4: The CMA enforces competition law, not data protection.

The Regulation of Financial Services.q: Which body provides oversight of pensions and occupational schemes?
The Regulation of Financial Services.w: The Pensions Regulator oversees occupational pension schemes, ensuring trustees meet governance and funding responsibilities.

n.1: The FCA regulates personal pensions and conduct, not occupational scheme trustees.
n.2: The Bank oversees systemic risks, not pension scheme governance.
n.3: The PRA supervises insurers, not occupational pension schemes.
n.4: The CMA focuses on competition, not pension oversight.

Prioritising volume of campaigns over clarity
Allowing sales staff to write promotions without oversight
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Clear, fair, and not misleading communications are reinforced when leaders ensure compliance independently reviews all promotions.

n.1: Suppressing disclosures undermines fair communications.
n.2: Targeting vulnerable clients is contrary to Principle 7.
n.3: Volume without clarity undermines obligations.
n.4: Lack of oversight increases risk of misleading promotions.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: Which leadership initiative best embeds cultural resilience to regulatory change?
o: Investing in continuous staff training on ethics and conduct
Delegating culture entirely to external consultants
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Ongoing training ensures staff understand evolving regulatory expectations, embedding resilience in culture.

n.1: Suppressing compliance findings undermines trust and resilience.
n.2: Transparency is critical; avoiding it undermines culture.
n.3: Culture cannot be outsourced entirely to consultants.
n.4: Cost-cutting without training weakens cultural resilience.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: Why is leadership ownership of culture essential under Consumer Duty?
o: Because outcomes for customers depend on senior accountability
Because it guarantees regulator fines will not occur
Because it allows ethics to be outsourced to consultants
Because it eliminates the need for client disclosures
Because it ensures all clients achieve identical returns
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Consumer Duty places cultural responsibility at board level. Leadership ownership ensures customer outcomes are central to governance.

n.1: Fines may still occur; accountability reduces but does not eliminate risk.
n.2: Culture cannot be outsourced; leadership must own it.
n.3: Disclosures remain mandatory regardless of culture.
n.4: Returns vary by client; culture ensures fairness, not identical outcomes.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: What obligation under Principle 1 is breached if directors manipulate valuation data to present stronger solvency?
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Principle 1 requires integrity. Manipulating valuation data undermines honesty and fairness in conduct.

n.1: Financial prudence requires adequate resources, but misrepresentation breaches integrity.
n.2: Management and control covers systems, whereas falsification is an integrity breach.
n.3: Customers’ interests relate to fair treatment, while data falsification concerns integrity.
n.4: Conflicts management is separate; misreporting solvency breaches integrity.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: Which principle requires client money to be segregated and reconciled promptly?
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Principle 10 requires safeguarding client money and custody assets through segregation and prompt reconciliation.

n.1: Relations with regulators address cooperation, not client-money safeguards.
n.2: Customers’ interests is wider fair treatment, whereas segregation is a specific asset safeguard.
n.3: Communications obligations are separate from safeguarding client money.
n.4: Management and control supports systems, but asset safeguarding is specific under Principle 10.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: What leadership-driven factor most strengthens resilience to conduct risk?
o: Embedding ethical values consistently across functions
Avoiding board discussions of cultural weaknesses
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Consistent reinforcement of ethical values builds resilience to misconduct, reducing systemic conduct risk.

n.1: Suppressing misconduct data hides risks, weakening resilience.
n.2: Accountability cannot rest solely with compliance; leadership must own culture.
n.3: Profit-only priorities undermine ethical resilience.
n.4: Avoiding cultural weaknesses leaves risks unaddressed.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: Which requirement under SM&CR reinforces accountability for client outcomes?
o: Fitness and propriety assessments of certified staff
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Fitness and propriety assessments ensure certified staff can carry out their roles responsibly, supporting fair outcomes for clients.

n.1: Conduct Rules still apply to all staff.
n.2: Capital adequacy is a prudential requirement, not specific to SM&CR accountability.
n.3: Duties cannot be delegated to regulators.
n.4: Reporting requirements are unchanged by fitness assessments.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: How can leadership tone influence Principle 1 outcomes?
o: By modelling honesty and integrity throughout the organisation
By tolerating misconduct in pursuit of growth
By promoting secrecy in compliance reporting
By focusing only on quarterly profit targets
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Principle 1 requires integrity. Leadership that models honesty and ethical behaviour drives organisational integrity.

n.1: Tolerating misconduct undermines cultural integrity.
n.2: Discouraging transparency breaches honesty obligations.
n.3: Promoting secrecy undermines regulator trust.
n.4: Profit-only focus conflicts with integrity obligations.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: Where should primary accountability for culture and controls sit to satisfy Principle 3?
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Principle 3 expects senior management and the governing body to ensure robust systems, effective controls, and sound risk management.

n.1: Outsourcing does not transfer accountability, whereas the governing body retains responsibility for systems and controls.
n.2: Compliance supports oversight, whereas overall accountability rests with senior management and the governing body.
n.3: Front-office participation is important, whereas accountability is held by the governing body.
n.4: Manufacturers have duties, whereas firm-wide control accountability sits with the governing body.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: Which principle ensures a firm maintains adequate liquidity to protect policyholder claims?
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Principle 4 requires adequate financial resources, ensuring firms can meet obligations like policyholder claims.

n.1: Integrity governs honesty, not liquidity adequacy.
n.2: Conflicts of interest address fairness, not liquidity adequacy.
n.3: Relationships of trust address suitability, not financial resources.
n.4: Market conduct governs trading fairness, not liquidity adequacy.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: What leadership quality supports Principle 7 compliance in vulnerable-customer communications?
o: Emphasising clarity and fairness in all disclosures
Suppressing warnings to avoid deterring sales
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Principle 7 requires communications to be clear and fair. Leaders must emphasise accessibility for vulnerable customers.

n.1: Jargon reduces clarity and breaches Principle 7 obligations.
n.2: Suppressing warnings misleads clients and breaches fairness.
n.3: Style without substance undermines clarity and fairness.
n.4: Accountability for communications remains with the firm, not distributors.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: What must firms demonstrate when certifying staff under the Certification Regime?
o: That they remain fit and proper for their roles
That the firm has achieved profit targets
That clients have experienced positive returns
That prudential ratios are above requirements
That all complaints have been resolved
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Certification requires evidence that individuals continue to be fit and proper, with integrity, competence, and capability to protect clients.

n.1: Profit targets are commercial, not certification standards.
n.2: Returns vary and are not a certification requirement.
n.3: Prudential ratios are unrelated to certification checks.
n.4: Complaints procedures are separate from certification obligations.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: What is required under Principle 2 when advising retail clients on complex derivatives?
o: Exercise due skill, care and diligence
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Principle 2 requires firms to act with due skill, care and diligence when advising, especially on complex products.

n.1: Profit margins disclosure is separate from the standard of skill, care and diligence.
n.2: Tax advice may be relevant but is not the duty defined under Principle 2.
n.3: Guarantees are rarely permissible and not the essence of Principle 2.
n.4: Execution-only removes advice, whereas Principle 2 governs diligence when advice is given.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: Why are annual fitness and propriety assessments important for certified staff?
o: They ensure staff remain capable and trustworthy
They exempt firms from regulator supervision
They eliminate the need for training programmes
They replace all other compliance obligations
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Annual fitness assessments ensure certified staff are competent, honest, and suitable to perform roles without risking client detriment.

n.1: Performance is market-driven and cannot be guaranteed by assessments.
n.2: Supervision continues regardless of assessments.
n.3: Training remains essential alongside certification.
n.4: Other compliance obligations still apply in addition to certification.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: What is a likely outcome when leadership suppresses negative cultural audit findings?
o: Increased regulatory risk and potential enforcement
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Suppressing cultural weaknesses increases regulatory risk, as issues remain hidden and unresolved until enforcement action.

n.1: Transparency is reduced, not improved, by suppression.
n.2: Compliance weakens if issues are ignored.
n.3: Openness declines if negative findings are hidden.
n.4: Misconduct risks increase, not reduce, under suppression.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: Which Conduct Rule requires staff to act with due skill, care and diligence?
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Individual Conduct Rule 2 requires staff to act with due skill, care and diligence in their roles.

n.1: Rule 1 requires acting with integrity, not diligence.
n.2: Rule 3 requires staff to be open and cooperative with regulators.
n.3: Senior Manager Rule 1 focuses on ensuring the firm is controlled effectively.
n.4: Senior Manager Rule 4 requires disclosure of regulatory breaches.

Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.q: How does leadership shape Principle 9 compliance in advice delivery?
o: By ensuring suitability frameworks are enforced
By prioritising sales over client interests
By limiting advice records to positive outcomes
By discouraging escalation of unsuitable advice
By delegating suitability decisions to untrained staff
Financial Regulators’ Ethical & Fair Out.w: Principle 9 requires suitable advice. Leadership must enforce frameworks ensuring staff consistently provide appropriate recommendations.

n.1: Sales-driven leadership undermines suitability obligations.
n.2: Incomplete advice records prevent proper oversight.
n.3: Discouraging escalation weakens trust in suitability systems.
n.4: Untrained staff cannot meet suitability obligations under Principle 9.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which funding model supports the FSCS?
o: Levies on authorised financial services firms
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The FSCS is funded by levies raised from authorised financial services firms within different funding classes.

n.1: Government taxation does not directly fund the FSCS.
n.2: Consumers do not pay subscriptions to the FSCS.
n.3: Insurance premiums fund policies, not FSCS itself.
n.4: Levies are mandatory, not voluntary contributions.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What compensation does the FSCS provide for claims relating to investment business?
o: Up to £85,000 per person per firm
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The FSCS provides compensation up to £85,000 per eligible claimant per failed investment firm.

n.1: Compensation is capped, not unlimited.
n.2: 90% applies in some insurance claims, not investment business.
n.3: £25,000 is below the current statutory limit.
n.4: £50,000 was the old limit, increased to £85,000.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which statement best describes PRA Fundamental Rule 5?
o: A firm must have effective risk strategies and risk management systems
A firm must pay due regard to its customers’ information needs
A firm must maintain adequate capital resources
A firm must conduct its business with integrity
A firm must deal with regulators in an open and co-operative way
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Fundamental Rule 5 requires a firm to have effective risk strategies and risk management systems appropriate to its business.

n.1: This refers to FCA Principle 7 on client communications, not PRA Rule 5.
n.2: Adequate capital resources are covered in PRA Fundamental Rule 4.
n.3: Integrity is Principle 1 (FCA), not PRA Rule 5.
n.4: Openness with regulators is Fundamental Rule 7, not Rule 5.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which FCA Principle requires firms to manage their business responsibly with adequate risk management systems?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Principle 3 requires firms to take reasonable care to organise and control their affairs responsibly with adequate risk management systems.

n.1: Principle 2 deals with skill, care and diligence, not organisation and systems.
n.2: Principle 5 covers market conduct, not internal organisation.
n.3: Principle 8 is about conflicts of interest, not overall organisation.
n.4: Principle 10 concerns client asset protection, not systems and controls.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which FCA Principle applies when a firm must take reasonable care to ensure the suitability of its advice?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Principle 9 requires firms to take reasonable care to ensure the suitability of their advice and discretionary decisions for any customer entitled to rely upon their judgment.

n.1: Principle 2 concerns skill, care and diligence generally, not suitability of advice specifically.
n.2: Principle 4 relates to financial prudence, not suitability.
n.3: Principle 6 is about treating customers fairly, which is broader than advice suitability.
n.4: Principle 11 requires openness with regulators, not suitability of advice.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Under SM&CR, what is the Conduct Rule that applies to all employees?
o: Report all pay details to HMRC
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The first Individual Conduct Rule requires all employees to act with integrity in carrying out their role.

n.1: Misleading the media is not explicitly listed as a Conduct Rule; integrity covers broader behaviour.
n.2: HMRC reporting is a tax obligation, not a Conduct Rule.
n.3: Shareholder returns are not prioritised within the Conduct Rules.
n.4: Fee maximisation is not a Conduct Rule; integrity governs conduct instead.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What happens if a consumer rejects a Financial Ombudsman Service decision?
o: They may still pursue the matter through the courts
The case is automatically referred to the FCA
The decision is escalated to the Upper Tribunal
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: If a complainant rejects a FOS decision, they are free to pursue the claim through the courts, as the Ombudsman’s decision is not binding on them.

n.1: FOS decisions are only binding on firms if accepted by the complainant.
n.2: The FCA does not take over individual complaint cases.
n.3: The FSCS is unrelated unless a firm fails; FOS rejection does not trigger FSCS compensation.
n.4: The Upper Tribunal hears appeals against regulators, not FOS rejections.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Where must responsibility for outsourced critical functions be recorded under SM&CR?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: SM&CR requires clear allocation of responsibilities, documented in the firm’s Responsibility Map.

n.1: Payslips are HR artefacts, whereas SM&CR mapping belongs in the Responsibility Map.
n.2: Factsheets describe products, not governance accountabilities required by SM&CR.
n.3: Marketing policy addresses promotions, while responsibilities must appear on the Responsibility Map.
n.4: Public websites are not the mandated repository; SM&CR requires an internal Responsibility Map.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the FSCS compensation limit for claims relating to pensions advice?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: For pensions advice claims, FSCS compensation is up to £85,000 per eligible person per failed firm.

n.1: £50,000 was the previous limit, now increased.
n.2: £150,000 is higher than the statutory FSCS limit.
n.3: £35,000 is an outdated figure.
n.4: Cover is capped, not unlimited.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which is an example of a red flag indicator of money laundering?
o: Unusually complex ownership structures with no clear purpose
Customers providing clear and consistent identification
Regular small payments from local clients
Clients responding promptly to due diligence requests
Routine payroll transactions by UK employers
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Unnecessarily complex ownership structures with no clear economic rationale are considered a red flag for potential money laundering.

n.1: Clear identification is a positive sign, not a red flag.
n.2: Regular small payments are generally normal activity.
n.3: Prompt responses to CDD are a positive indicator, not a red flag.
n.4: Routine payroll transactions are normal and not red flags.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which organisation issues Joint Money Laundering Steering Group (JMLSG) guidance?
o: UK financial services industry body consortium
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The JMLSG is an industry-led body that produces detailed guidance on how firms can meet UK AML requirements in practice, endorsed by HM Treasury.

n.1: The FCA endorses but does not issue JMLSG guidance; it is industry-led.
n.2: HM Treasury endorses the guidance but does not author it alone.
n.3: The ECB does not issue UK AML guidance.
n.4: Parliament does not issue JMLSG guidance; it is industry produced.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which principle under UK GDPR requires personal data to be collected for specified, explicit purposes?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Purpose limitation means data must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a way incompatible with those purposes.

n.1: Data minimisation is about collecting only necessary data, not purpose limitation.
n.2: Storage limitation covers retaining data only as long as necessary.
n.3: Accuracy requires personal data to be kept up to date, not limited to purposes.
n.4: Integrity and confidentiality address security, not purposes.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What type of firm failure would trigger FSCS protection for deposits?
o: A firm failing to respond to complaints within 8 weeks
A firm being fined by the FCA
A bank refusing to lend to small businesses
A firm’s share price declining on the stock exchange
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: FSCS protection is triggered when an authorised deposit-taker, such as a bank or building society, becomes insolvent and cannot repay deposits.

n.1: Complaint handling failures do not activate FSCS protection.
n.2: Regulatory fines do not trigger FSCS compensation.
n.3: Lending policy decisions do not trigger FSCS protection.
n.4: Market value losses are not protected by FSCS.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which body is responsible for publishing the PRA Rulebook?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The PRA publishes the PRA Rulebook, which sets prudential requirements for regulated firms.

n.1: The FCA publishes the FCA Handbook, not the PRA Rulebook.
n.2: HM Treasury sets government policy, not the PRA Rulebook.
n.3: The FPC sets macroprudential policy, not detailed rules for firms.
n.4: The EBA issues EU standards, but the PRA Rulebook is domestic UK regulation.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which class of FSCS protection applies to deposits, insurance, investments, and home finance?
o: Separate funding classes with tailored limits
Single universal class with unlimited cover
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The FSCS operates through different funding classes — deposits, insurance, investments, home finance — each with specific limits and rules.

n.1: Cover is capped and differentiated, not unlimited universal cover.
n.2: Insurance is covered but so are other categories like deposits and investments.
n.3: Deposits are one class, not the only one.
n.4: Levies are collected across funding classes, not as one flat pool.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which body resolves complaints about pensions schemes not covered by the FOS?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The Pensions Ombudsman deals with complaints about maladministration and disputes in occupational and personal pension schemes not covered by the FOS.

n.1: The FSCS provides compensation for failed firms, not pension disputes.
n.2: The Upper Tribunal hears appeals against regulator decisions, not pensions disputes.
n.3: The PRA sets prudential rules, not pension dispute resolution.
n.4: The NCA handles crime intelligence, not pensions complaints.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which PRA Fundamental Rule requires a firm to conduct business prudently?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Fundamental Rule 6 requires a firm to conduct its business in a prudent manner.

n.1: Rule 2 deals with skill, care and diligence, not prudence.
n.2: Rule 3 requires adequate systems and organisation, not prudence.
n.3: Rule 4 requires adequate capital resources, not prudence.
n.4: Rule 7 is about openness with regulators, not prudence.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the role of the National Crime Agency in AML?
o: To receive and analyse suspicious activity reports
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The NCA receives and analyses SARs, acting as the UK’s financial intelligence unit in the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing.

n.1: Financial conduct is regulated by the FCA, not the NCA.
n.2: The ICO enforces data protection, not the NCA.
n.3: Prudential requirements fall to the PRA, not the NCA.
n.4: Legislation is enacted by Parliament, not the NCA.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What compensation is available under the FSCS for deposits in credit unions?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The FSCS protects deposits up to £85,000 per person per credit union, the same as for banks and building societies.

n.1: £50,000 was the former limit, increased to £85,000.
n.2: Protection is capped; it is not unlimited.
n.3: £25,000 is too low and not a statutory figure.
n.4: 90% capped protection applies to certain insurance, not deposits.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: How long must firms keep complaint records for DISP purposes if they are subject to the Financial Ombudsman Service?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: DISP requires firms covered by the Financial Ombudsman Service to keep complaint records for at least three years.

n.1: Six years applies to some other financial records, not DISP complaints.
n.2: One year is shorter than the DISP requirement.
n.3: Indefinite retention is not mandated by DISP.
n.4: Two years is below the minimum required retention period.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which UK authority enforces breaches of financial sanctions?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) is responsible for enforcing breaches of UK financial sanctions.

n.1: The FCA regulates conduct but does not enforce sanctions breaches.
n.2: The SFO prosecutes fraud, not sanctions breaches.
n.3: The ICO enforces data protection, not sanctions.
n.4: The PRA focuses on prudential standards, not sanctions.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which FSCS protection applies to deposits held in foreign branches of UK-authorised banks within the EEA?
o: They are covered by the FSCS up to £85,000
They are only covered if over £100,000
They are covered only if reported to HM Treasury
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Deposits in EEA branches of UK-authorised banks are protected by the FSCS up to £85,000 per eligible claimant.

n.1: They are covered, subject to the £85,000 limit.
n.2: The £100,000 figure is not the statutory limit.
n.3: Cover is capped; it is not unlimited.
n.4: Protection does not require HM Treasury reporting; it applies automatically.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the FCA’s Principle 10 concerned with?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Principle 10 requires firms to arrange adequate protection for clients’ assets when they are responsible for them.

n.1: Proper market conduct is Principle 5, not Principle 10.
n.2: Treating customers fairly is Principle 6, not Principle 10.
n.3: Financial promotions rules are separate conduct standards, not Principle 10.
n.4: Remuneration is subject to remuneration codes, not Principle 10.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which is a lawful basis for processing sensitive ‘special category’ data under UK GDPR?
o: Explicit consent of the data subject
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Special category data, such as health or biometric data, requires explicit consent or another special condition under UK GDPR.

n.1: Contractual necessity does not in itself permit special category processing.
n.2: Marketing interest is not sufficient for sensitive data.
n.3: Automatic collection without basis breaches UK GDPR.
n.4: Internal convenience is never a lawful basis for special category data.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What does the data protection principle of ‘data minimisation’ require?
o: Collecting only data necessary for the stated purpose
Ensuring data is accurate and kept up to date
Storing data only as long as necessary
Keeping data secure against unauthorised access
Processing data lawfully, fairly and transparently
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Data minimisation requires firms to ensure personal data collected is adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purpose.

n.1: Accuracy is a separate principle, not minimisation.
n.2: Storage limitation is a different GDPR principle.
n.3: Security relates to integrity and confidentiality, not minimisation.
n.4: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency are a separate principle, not minimisation.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Where are UK prudential standards for insurers primarily codified?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Insurer prudential requirements are set out primarily in the PRA Rulebook.

n.1: The FCA Handbook focuses on conduct rules, whereas insurer prudential rules sit in the PRA Rulebook.
n.2: MiFID II governs investment services, while domestic prudential rules for insurers are in the PRA Rulebook.
n.3: Tribunal decisions resolve disputes; they do not codify prudential requirements like the PRA Rulebook does.
n.4: CMA guidance addresses competition issues, not prudential standards set in the PRA Rulebook.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which regulator’s objectives include ensuring firms can fail in an orderly way without disrupting the system?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The PRA’s objectives include promoting the safety and soundness of firms so that they can fail in an orderly way without systemic disruption.

n.1: The FOS resolves disputes between customers and firms; it does not regulate firm failure.
n.2: The FCA’s Market Oversight focuses on market abuse, not orderly failure of firms.
n.3: The Competition Appeal Tribunal handles competition cases, not prudential objectives.
n.4: The Pensions Regulator supervises pensions schemes, not banking firm failures.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which principle of UK GDPR requires firms to collect only data that is necessary?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Data minimisation requires that only data necessary for the specified purpose is collected, avoiding excessive or irrelevant personal data.

n.1: Purpose limitation restricts the use of data to defined purposes, not its amount.
n.2: Accuracy ensures data is correct, not minimised.
n.3: Integrity and confidentiality relate to security, not minimisation.
n.4: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency address legality and openness, not minimisation.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which body can impose administrative fines for data protection breaches in the UK?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The ICO is the UK regulator empowered to impose administrative fines for breaches of the Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR.

n.1: The FCA does not enforce data protection legislation.
n.2: The PRA regulates prudential matters, not data protection.
n.3: The NCA handles financial crime intelligence, not data protection enforcement.
n.4: The SFO prosecutes serious fraud, not data protection breaches.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the maximum administrative fine under UK GDPR for the most serious breaches?
o: £500,000 as under the old Data Protection Act 1998
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 allow fines up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual worldwide turnover, whichever is higher, for serious breaches.

n.1: This refers to lower-tier infringements, not the maximum.
n.2: £5 million understates the statutory maximum.
n.3: £1 million is too low for serious GDPR breaches.
n.4: £500,000 was the maximum under the 1998 Act, replaced by higher GDPR fines.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the time limit for consumers to refer complaints to the FOS after receiving a firm’s final response?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Consumers have six months from the date of the firm’s final response letter to refer a complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

n.1: Three months is too short; the rule allows six months.
n.2: One year exceeds the permitted referral time frame.
n.3: Two weeks is far shorter than the six months allowed.
n.4: There is a clear statutory time limit; it is not open-ended.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the role of the Upper Tribunal in relation to FCA and PRA decisions?
o: To hear references and appeals against certain regulatory decisions
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber) hears references and appeals against certain FCA and PRA regulatory decisions.

n.1: Compensation to consumers is handled by FOS or FSCS, not the Tribunal.
n.2: The FSCS is overseen by the FCA and PRA, not the Tribunal.
n.3: Promotions guidance is issued by the FCA, not the Tribunal.
n.4: The Tribunal does not register financial products.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which type of money laundering involves concealing the origin of funds by layering complex transactions?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Layering is the stage where illicit funds are separated from their origin through complex transactions designed to obscure the audit trail.

n.1: Placement is the initial introduction of illicit funds into the system, not layering.
n.2: Integration is the final stage, not the transaction layering stage.
n.3: Structuring refers to breaking down transactions, not the full layering process.
n.4: Commingling means mixing illicit funds with legitimate funds, not layering.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Under SM&CR, who is ultimately accountable for the firm’s conduct and culture?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Under SM&CR, Senior Managers hold ultimate accountability for conduct, culture, and regulatory compliance within their areas of responsibility.

n.1: Middle managers may support implementation but ultimate accountability lies with Senior Managers.
n.2: Consultants can advise but do not hold accountability under SM&CR.
n.3: Customer service staff are not accountable for the firm’s overall culture under SM&CR.
n.4: External auditors provide assurance but accountability lies with Senior Managers.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Who sets the PRA Fundamental Rules for prudentially regulated firms?
o: Bank of England Monetary Policy Committee
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The PRA issues its Fundamental Rules within the PRA Rulebook for prudentially regulated firms.

n.1: The FCA publishes Principles for Businesses, not the PRA Fundamental Rules, whereas the PRA sets those prudential rules.
n.2: HM Treasury sets legislation and policy, not the PRA’s Fundamental Rules, which are issued by the prudential regulator.
n.3: The MPC sets interest rates, not prudential rules; the PRA issues the Fundamental Rules.
n.4: The Upper Tribunal hears regulatory appeals, not creates prudential rules, which the PRA sets.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which FSCS protection applies to non-compulsory general insurance policies such as home insurance?
o: 90% of the claim with no upper limit
100% of the claim with no upper limit
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: FSCS protection for most non-compulsory general insurance policies, such as home insurance, is 90% of the claim with no upper limit.

n.1: 100% applies to compulsory insurance and long-term insurance, not non-compulsory general policies.
n.2: £85,000 is the limit for deposits and investments, not general insurance.
n.3: £50,000 is outdated and not current FSCS protection.
n.4: 75% capped at £100,000 is not an FSCS rule.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the effect of accepting a Financial Ombudsman Service decision by a complainant?
o: The decision becomes binding on both parties
The decision is reviewed by the FCA
The complainant must pay case fees
The case is automatically referred to court
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Once a complainant accepts a FOS decision, it becomes binding on both the firm and the complainant, enforceable in court if necessary.

n.1: The decision is not voluntary once accepted; it is binding.
n.2: The FCA does not review FOS decisions.
n.3: Complainants do not pay case fees; firms fund the service.
n.4: Court involvement only arises for enforcement, not automatic referral.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which rule source in the FCA Handbook sets out the operation of the FSCS?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The COMP sourcebook of the FCA Handbook sets out the rules for the operation of the Financial Services Compensation Scheme.

n.1: COBS covers conduct of business, not compensation scheme rules.
n.2: DISP covers complaints handling, not FSCS rules.
n.3: SYSC covers systems and controls, not FSCS.
n.4: CASS relates to client assets, not compensation schemes.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Under AML rules, when must customer due diligence be performed?
o: Before establishing a business relationship or carrying out a transaction
Only after a suspicious activity report is filed
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Customer due diligence must be completed before establishing a business relationship or carrying out a relevant transaction, ensuring proper checks are in place.

n.1: CDD must occur before, not after, suspicious activity is reported.
n.2: Ten-year intervals are non-compliant; checks must be risk-based and ongoing.
n.3: CDD is not optional based on regulator request; it is mandatory.
n.4: Audits may review CDD, but due diligence must occur earlier.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the FSCS compensation limit for general insurance claims such as compulsory motor insurance?
o: 100% of the claim with no upper limit
90% of the claim with no upper limit
75% of the claim with a £100,000 cap
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: FSCS provides 100% cover for compulsory classes of insurance such as motor insurance, with no upper monetary limit.

n.1: 90% cover applies to other types of insurance, not compulsory motor.
n.2: £85,000 is the limit for deposits and investments, not compulsory insurance.
n.3: £50,000 is outdated and incorrect here.
n.4: 75% protection does not reflect FSCS rules.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the role of a Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO)?
o: To receive and assess internal suspicious activity reports
To approve all client account openings
To prosecute offenders in criminal courts
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: An MLRO is the designated officer in a firm responsible for receiving internal reports of suspicious activity, assessing them, and deciding whether to file a SAR with the NCA.

n.1: AML legislation is set by government, not the MLRO.
n.2: Client account approvals may involve due diligence, but the MLRO’s role is suspicious activity reporting.
n.3: Prosecutions are conducted by authorities, not MLROs.
n.4: Product strategy is unrelated to the MLRO function.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the current FSCS limit for protected deposits per person per authorised bank?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The FSCS protects deposits up to £85,000 per eligible person, per authorised bank or building society.

n.1: £50,000 was the former limit prior to 2010; it has since increased.
n.2: £100,000 is not the correct FSCS protected deposit limit.
n.3: £150,000 exceeds the statutory deposit protection limit.
n.4: £25,000 understates the protection available.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What does the term ‘beneficial ownership’ mean in AML regulation?
o: The natural person who ultimately owns or controls a customer
The individual who benefits from a retail promotion
The solicitor acting as nominee for a client
Any director listed at Companies House
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Beneficial ownership refers to the natural person(s) who ultimately own or control a customer, or on whose behalf a transaction is conducted.

n.1: Retail promotions are unrelated to AML beneficial ownership rules.
n.2: Nominee solicitors may act for clients but do not define beneficial ownership.
n.3: Not all directors are beneficial owners; it depends on control and ownership.
n.4: The compliance officer manages AML processes but is not the beneficial owner.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which lawful basis under UK GDPR permits processing personal data to fulfil contractual obligations?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Processing is lawful under UK GDPR if it is necessary for the performance of a contract with the data subject, such as providing services or fulfilling orders.

n.1: Legitimate interests apply when a firm balances interests, not contract fulfilment.
n.2: Consent may apply in other cases but is not required if processing is contractually necessary.
n.3: Legal obligation applies to compliance with laws, not contractual performance.
n.4: Vital interests relate to life-and-death scenarios, not contracts.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which UK GDPR principle requires firms to process data lawfully, fairly and transparently?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires firms to process data in a manner that is lawful, fair and transparent to individuals.

n.1: Purpose limitation relates to restricting data to specific purposes, not fairness.
n.2: Accuracy concerns correctness of data, not fairness.
n.3: Storage limitation is about duration of data retention, not fairness.
n.4: Integrity and confidentiality address security, not fairness.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which PRA Fundamental Rule requires a firm to maintain adequate financial resources?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: PRA Fundamental Rule 4 requires firms to maintain adequate financial resources appropriate to the risks they face.

n.1: Rule 2 is about skill, care and diligence, not capital resources.
n.2: Rule 3 concerns organising affairs responsibly, not financial resources.
n.3: Rule 5 covers risk strategies, not financial resources directly.
n.4: Rule 7 requires openness with regulators, not capital adequacy.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is ‘integration’ in the money laundering process?
o: The reintroduction of laundered funds into the legitimate economy
The initial placement of illicit cash into the system
The layering of transactions to obscure origin
The concealment of a PEP’s identity
The structuring of deposits below thresholds
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Integration is the final stage of money laundering where illicit funds are reintroduced into the economy as apparently legitimate assets.

n.1: Placement is the first stage, not integration.
n.2: Layering is the second stage, not the final one.
n.3: Concealing a PEP’s identity is a risk factor, not integration.
n.4: Structuring refers to breaking up deposits, not the integration stage.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Under SM&CR, what is the function of the Certification Regime?
o: To ensure individuals in significant harm functions are assessed as fit and proper
To register new products with the FCA
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The Certification Regime ensures individuals performing roles that could cause significant harm to customers or the market are fit and proper, assessed at least annually by the firm.

n.1: Product registration is not part of the Certification Regime.
n.2: Compensation is provided by the FSCS or FOS, not through Certification.
n.3: Financial promotions approval is a compliance function, not Certification.
n.4: Auditors are appointed separately, not under Certification.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the FSCS compensation limit for investment claims?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The FSCS provides compensation for investment business up to £85,000 per eligible claimant per failed firm.

n.1: £50,000 was the old limit before being raised to £85,000.
n.2: £100,000 is above the statutory limit.
n.3: £35,000 was a much older limit, now superseded.
n.4: £10,000 significantly understates the available compensation.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the primary purpose of customer due diligence under AML rules?
o: To identify and verify customers to prevent misuse of the financial system
To collect marketing information for cross-selling
To qualify for FCA fee reductions
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: CDD ensures firms identify and verify customers to reduce the risk of criminals misusing the financial system for money laundering or terrorist financing.

n.1: Marketing information is not the purpose of CDD.
n.2: Pricing consistency is unrelated to AML obligations.
n.3: Client satisfaction measures are not part of AML CDD.
n.4: FCA fees are unrelated to CDD obligations.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which scheme protects eligible claimants if an authorised investment firm fails?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) provides compensation to eligible claimants if authorised firms fail, including investment and deposit takers.

n.1: The FOS resolves complaints but does not provide compensation for firm failures.
n.2: The PRA supervises prudential matters, not consumer compensation.
n.3: The Pension Protection Fund covers pension schemes, not general investment firm failures.
n.4: The Competition Appeal Tribunal does not operate compensation schemes.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which FCA Principle requires clarity and fairness in client communications?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Principle 7 requires firms to pay due regard to information needs and communicate in a way that is clear, fair and not misleading.

n.1: Principle 3 relates to risk management and organisation, not communications.
n.2: Principle 2 is about skill, care and diligence, not communications clarity.
n.3: Principle 9 concerns customers’ relationships of trust, not communication rules.
n.4: Principle 10 relates to conflicts of interest, not communications.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Under UK GDPR, what is the principle of ‘accuracy’?
o: Personal data must be accurate and kept up to date
Data must be kept only as long as needed
Only data strictly necessary must be collected
Data must be processed lawfully and fairly
Data must be protected from unauthorised access
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The accuracy principle requires firms to ensure personal data is accurate and kept up to date, correcting inaccuracies without delay.

n.1: This describes storage limitation, not accuracy.
n.2: This refers to data minimisation, not accuracy.
n.3: This is the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle, not accuracy.
n.4: This is integrity and confidentiality, not accuracy.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which disputes fall outside the jurisdiction of the Financial Ombudsman Service?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The FOS only considers disputes involving authorised firms; complaints about unauthorised firms are outside its jurisdiction.

n.1: Mis-sold investments are within FOS jurisdiction.
n.2: Insurance complaints can be referred to the FOS.
n.3: Consumer credit disputes fall within FOS scope.
n.4: Mortgage complaints are within FOS jurisdiction.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the FSCS protection limit for mortgage advice and arranging claims?
o: 100% of the claim with no limit
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: FSCS protection for mortgage advice and arranging claims is £85,000 per eligible claimant per firm.

n.1: £50,000 was the old limit; the current limit is £85,000.
n.2: Unlimited cover applies only to certain insurance, not mortgages.
n.3: £25,000 is not the statutory figure.
n.4: 90% capped cover does not apply to mortgage advice claims.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which PRA Fundamental Rule requires firms to have effective risk strategies and risk management systems?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: PRA Fundamental Rule 5 requires firms to have effective risk strategies and risk management systems suitable for their business model.

n.1: Rule 2 is about skill, care and diligence, not risk systems.
n.2: Rule 3 concerns organisation and control, not risk strategy.
n.3: Rule 4 is about adequate financial resources, not risk systems.
n.4: Rule 7 is about openness with regulators, not risk systems.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which UK GDPR principle requires firms to secure personal data against unauthorised access?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The integrity and confidentiality principle (security) requires personal data to be processed securely, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing.

n.1: Purpose limitation ensures data is collected only for explicit purposes, not security.
n.2: Accuracy requires data to be correct, not secure.
n.3: Data minimisation relates to limiting data collected, not security.
n.4: Storage limitation governs how long data is kept, not security.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the penalty for ‘tipping off’ under money laundering legislation?
o: Up to two years’ imprisonment and/or a fine
Immediate loss of FCA authorisation only
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Tipping off under POCA and MLR is punishable by up to two years’ imprisonment, a fine, or both.

n.1: Regulatory action may occur, but criminal penalties are set in statute.
n.2: Community service is not the statutory penalty for tipping off.
n.3: Civil damages are not the prescribed penalty under AML laws.
n.4: Political bans are unrelated to AML tipping off offences.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is ‘tipping off’ under money laundering legislation?
o: Informing a suspect that a suspicious activity report has been filed
Withdrawing cash in small amounts to avoid reporting
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Tipping off occurs when someone informs a suspect that a suspicious activity report has been made, potentially prejudicing an investigation.

n.1: Withdrawing cash in small amounts is structuring, not tipping off.
n.2: Commingling is mixing funds, not tipping off.
n.3: Ignoring activity may be a failure to act, but tipping off is active disclosure.
n.4: Falsifying records is separate misconduct, not tipping off.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which FCA Principle requires a firm to conduct business with due skill, care and diligence?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Principle 2 requires firms to conduct business with due skill, care and diligence.

n.1: Principle 5 is about observing proper standards of market conduct, not skill and diligence.
n.2: Principle 6 concerns treating customers fairly, not skill and diligence.
n.3: Principle 9 relates to customer relationships of trust, not skill and diligence.
n.4: Principle 11 requires openness with regulators, not skill and diligence.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which PRA Fundamental Rule requires a firm to act with integrity?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: PRA Fundamental Rule 1 requires firms to conduct their business with integrity.

n.1: Rule 2 relates to skill, care and diligence, not integrity.
n.2: Rule 3 requires organising affairs responsibly, not integrity.
n.3: Rule 4 concerns adequate capital, not integrity.
n.4: Rule 6 is about prudence, not integrity.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the primary purpose of the DISP sourcebook in the FCA Handbook?
o: To set rules for handling customer complaints
To regulate firms’ prudential capital requirements
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The DISP sourcebook sets out the rules and guidance for firms on handling customer complaints and referring unresolved issues to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

n.1: Prudential capital requirements are covered by the PRA and other FCA rules, not DISP.
n.2: Data protection is covered by UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act, not DISP.
n.3: Financial promotions standards are covered in COBS, not DISP.
n.4: Insider dealing offences are criminal matters, not DISP rules.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Under Consumer Duty, what outcome must firms ensure regarding communications?
o: Clients receive communications they can understand and act upon
Clients always receive the lowest cost option
Clients receive advice automatically with each product
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Consumer Duty requires communications that enable clients to understand and make informed decisions about products and services.

n.1: Maximum choice is not the obligation; clarity and usefulness of communications is the requirement.
n.2: Lowest cost is not always required; suitability and understanding are key.
n.3: Promotional messages alone do not meet the Consumer Duty standard.
n.4: Automatic advice is not required for every product; communications must simply be understandable.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: When are client money internal reconciliations required under CASS for standard methods?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: CASS requires daily internal reconciliations on business days when using standard client money methods.

n.1: Weekly reconciliation is insufficient, whereas CASS requires daily internal checks for standard methods.
n.2: Monthly timing is too infrequent, while CASS mandates daily internal reconciliations.
n.3: Quarterly cycles are non-compliant because CASS requires daily reconciliation.
n.4: Waiting for discrepancies is reactive; CASS requires proactive daily reconciliation.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which POCA offence involves using criminal property in day-to-day transactions?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Acquisition, use or possession of criminal property under POCA is an offence covering situations where individuals knowingly handle illicit funds in transactions.

n.1: Concealing covers disguising property, not using it.
n.2: Failure to disclose is about reporting suspicions, not use of property.
n.3: Tipping off involves warning suspects, not using property.
n.4: Negligence is not a defined POCA offence.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which FSCS protection applies to long-term insurance contracts such as life insurance?
o: 100% of the claim with no upper limit
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The FSCS covers 100% of claims arising from long-term insurance policies such as life insurance, with no monetary cap.

n.1: 90% applies to certain non-compulsory insurance classes, not long-term insurance.
n.2: 75% capped is not a recognised FSCS category.
n.3: £50,000 is below the true level of protection.
n.4: £25,000 is not the statutory limit for life policies.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: How long must firms attempt to resolve complaints internally before escalation to the FOS is permitted?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Firms must be given up to eight weeks to resolve complaints internally before consumers can escalate to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

n.1: Two weeks is shorter than the statutory period of eight weeks.
n.2: Three months exceeds the maximum allowed before escalation.
n.3: One month is shorter than the required eight weeks.
n.4: Six months is the consumer’s referral period, not the firm’s response period.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What management information best evidences pricing fairness under Consumer Duty?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Fair value assessments directly evaluate price and value, evidencing Consumer Duty pricing outcomes.

n.1: Openings volume reflects sales, whereas fair value assesses price and benefits alignment.
n.2: Follower growth is marketing reach, not evidence of fair price and value.
n.3: Commission totals indicate revenue, not whether customers receive fair value.
n.4: Bounce rate is web analytics, not a measure of Consumer Duty value outcomes.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Under SM&CR, what is the purpose of a Statement of Responsibilities?
o: To detail each Senior Manager’s specific responsibilities
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Each Senior Manager must have a Statement of Responsibilities showing clearly the areas they are accountable for under SM&CR.

n.1: Voting rights are corporate law issues, not SM&CR Statements of Responsibilities.
n.2: Client categorisation is covered under COBS, not SM&CR documentation.
n.3: Complaints procedures are part of DISP, not SM&CR Statements.
n.4: Remuneration is HR-related, not documented in Statements of Responsibilities.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which FSCS protection applies to deposits in authorised UK banks?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: FSCS protection for deposits is £85,000 per eligible claimant per authorised bank or building society.

n.1: £50,000 was the old limit, no longer in force.
n.2: £100,000 is not the statutory FSCS deposit limit.
n.3: £150,000 exceeds the statutory cap.
n.4: FSCS cover is capped, not unlimited.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Why does the FCA apply the principle of treating customers fairly?
o: To ensure customers’ interests are at the heart of how firms operate
To guarantee firms achieve maximum profit
To align UK firms with EU accounting standards
To encourage firms to outsource compliance
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Treating customers fairly ensures customers’ interests are central, leading to better outcomes and reinforcing trust in the financial system.

n.1: Profitability is not the aim; the focus is fair treatment and outcomes.
n.2: Regulatory costs are not the purpose; the goal is fairness.
n.3: Accounting standards alignment is not the aim of the FCA’s fair treatment principle.
n.4: Outsourcing compliance is not an objective of treating customers fairly.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the primary purpose of the FCA’s Principles for Businesses?
o: To act as high-level standards guiding firm behaviour
To replace all detailed rules in the FCA Handbook
To outline statutory duties of Parliament
To specify tax obligations for firms
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The Principles for Businesses set out high-level expectations that underpin detailed FCA rules and guide firm behaviour.

n.1: Principles do not replace detailed rules; they complement them as overarching standards.
n.2: Financial reporting templates are not included in the Principles.
n.3: Parliament’s statutory duties are not part of FCA Principles.
n.4: Tax obligations fall outside FCA Principles and are HMRC’s domain.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which UK body maintains the consolidated list of financial sanctions targets?
o: HM Treasury’s Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: HM Treasury’s Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) maintains the UK’s consolidated list of individuals and entities subject to financial sanctions.

n.1: The FCA regulates conduct but does not maintain the sanctions list.
n.2: The NCA receives SARs, not sanctions lists.
n.3: The Bank of England previously had this role but it is now handled by OFSI.
n.4: The ICO oversees data protection, not sanctions compliance.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which of the following is a type of complaint that can be considered under DISP rules?
o: General disputes between landlords and tenants
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: DISP applies to complaints about regulated financial services, such as mis-selling of investments or insurance products.

n.1: Landlord and tenant disputes are not within DISP scope.
n.2: Employment claims are dealt with by employment tribunals, not DISP.
n.3: Competition law is overseen by the CMA, not DISP.
n.4: Tax disputes are dealt with by HMRC and tribunals, not DISP.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Under AML rules, what is a politically exposed person (PEP)?
o: An individual entrusted with prominent public functions
A person who has defaulted on a mortgage
Any director of a UK company
A client with an adverse credit history
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: A PEP is someone entrusted with a prominent public function, such as heads of state or senior politicians, and presents higher AML risk.

n.1: Mortgage defaults are credit issues, not PEP status.
n.2: Company directors are not PEPs unless they hold political functions.
n.3: Adverse credit does not make someone a PEP.
n.4: Wealth alone does not define PEP status.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What FCA Principle is met when a firm maintains adequate financial resources?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Maintaining adequate financial resources aligns with FCA Principle 4, Financial Prudence.

n.1: Integrity concerns honesty and fairness, whereas adequate resources relate to Financial Prudence.
n.2: Customers’ Interests prioritises fair treatment, while adequate resources specifically address Financial Prudence.
n.3: Communications with Clients covers clarity of information, not capital adequacy, which is Financial Prudence.
n.4: Market Conduct concerns market standards, not resource adequacy, which is Financial Prudence.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which consumers are eligible to bring complaints to the FOS?
o: Retail consumers and certain small businesses
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: FOS eligibility extends to retail consumers and certain small businesses, charities and trusts, but not to large corporations or institutions.

n.1: Institutional investors are not covered under FOS eligibility rules.
n.2: Multinationals are not eligible complainants at the FOS.
n.3: Shareholder disputes are not within FOS remit.
n.4: Government agencies are not complainants for FOS purposes.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which authority is responsible for supervising data protection compliance in the UK?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) is the UK’s regulator for data protection and privacy, enforcing the Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR.

n.1: The FCA regulates financial conduct, not data protection.
n.2: The PRA regulates prudential standards, not data protection.
n.3: The NCA handles financial crime intelligence, not data protection.
n.4: HM Treasury sets financial policy, not data protection rules.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which piece of UK legislation is the primary framework for anti-money laundering obligations?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds Regulations 2017 are the primary UK AML framework, imposing obligations on firms to prevent and detect money laundering.

n.1: The Companies Act 2006 governs company law, not AML obligations.
n.2: The Financial Services Act 2012 focuses on regulatory structure and enforcement, not AML rules.
n.3: The Data Protection Act 2018 concerns handling of personal data, not AML obligations.
n.4: The Consumer Rights Act 2015 relates to consumer protection, not AML frameworks.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which regulator sets the rules for the Financial Ombudsman Service and FSCS?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The FCA is responsible for setting and maintaining the rules for both the FOS and FSCS in the FCA Handbook (DISP and COMP).

n.1: The PRA sets prudential standards, not dispute resolution rules.
n.2: The ICO regulates data protection, not FOS or FSCS.
n.3: The NCA handles crime intelligence, not compensation scheme rules.
n.4: OFSI enforces sanctions, not dispute resolution schemes.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which complaint handling rule requires firms to investigate complaints competently, diligently and impartially?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: DISP 1.4 requires firms to handle complaints promptly and fairly by investigating competently, diligently and impartially.

n.1: COBS 4.2 relates to financial promotions, not complaints handling.
n.2: PRIN 2.1 contains Principles for Businesses, not detailed complaint procedures.
n.3: SYSC 6.1 addresses compliance arrangements, not complaints handling.
n.4: CASS 7.12 deals with client money rules, not complaints.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Why does the FCA apply the principle of proportionality in its regulation?
o: To ensure requirements are applied in a way appropriate to the size and complexity of a firm
To exempt large firms from regulatory obligations
To impose identical rules regardless of firm type
To prioritise tax collection over conduct issues
To align solely with international accounting standards
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Proportionality ensures regulatory requirements reflect the scale, nature and complexity of the firm’s activities.

n.1: Large firms are not exempt; they face stricter requirements under proportionality.
n.2: Identical rules regardless of type would contradict proportionality.
n.3: Tax collection is HMRC’s role, not a purpose of proportionality.
n.4: Accounting alignment is separate from FCA proportionality principles.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: When must a firm complete fitness and propriety certification for certified persons?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Under SM&CR, certification assessments must be completed at least annually for certified roles.

n.1: Three-year cycles are too infrequent, whereas SM&CR requires at least annual certification.
n.2: Initial hiring checks are insufficient alone, since SM&CR requires ongoing annual certification.
n.3: Complaints may trigger reviews, but SM&CR mandates routine annual certification regardless.
n.4: Twice yearly is not required; the minimum requirement is at least annually.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What document sets out the PRA’s expectations for firms’ risk management and governance?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The PRA Rulebook contains binding rules and supervisory expectations on governance and risk management for prudential firms.

n.1: The FCA Handbook deals mainly with conduct, not prudential risk management rules.
n.2: The FSCS guidance relates to compensation, not governance rules.
n.3: MiFID II is EU legislation on investment services, not PRA-specific rules.
n.4: White papers outline policy proposals, not regulatory rules.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What does the data protection principle of ‘storage limitation’ require?
o: Data must not be kept longer than necessary for its purpose
Data must be accurate and up to date
Data must be processed fairly and lawfully
Data must be limited to what is necessary
Data must be encrypted at all times
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The storage limitation principle requires firms not to retain personal data for longer than necessary for the purpose for which it was collected.

n.1: Accuracy is a separate GDPR principle.
n.2: Fairness and lawfulness are different principles.
n.3: Data minimisation covers limiting collection, not retention.
n.4: Encryption supports security, but is not the same as storage limitation.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which types of claims are excluded from FSCS protection?
o: Claims relating to unregulated collective investment schemes
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: FSCS does not cover claims involving unregulated collective investment schemes, which are outside the scope of authorised business.

n.1: Deposits with authorised banks are protected up to £85,000.
n.2: Compulsory motor insurance claims are fully covered.
n.3: Long-term insurance claims are covered in full with no limit.
n.4: Pension advice claims are covered up to £85,000 per firm.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the penalty for breaching the UK Data Protection Act 2018?
o: Administrative fines up to £17.5m or 4% of global turnover
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The UK Data Protection Act 2018, aligned with UK GDPR, allows fines up to the greater of £17.5m or 4% of annual worldwide turnover.

n.1: Imprisonment is not the main penalty; fines are the primary sanction.
n.2: Parliamentary charters are unrelated to data protection breaches.
n.3: Community service is not a statutory penalty for data breaches.
n.4: FSCS cover relates to compensation, not data protection enforcement.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: What is the final stage of money laundering called?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Integration is the final stage of money laundering, where laundered funds are reintroduced into the legitimate economy appearing as clean assets.

n.1: Placement is the first stage, not the final one.
n.2: Layering is the second stage, not the final one.
n.3: Structuring refers to transaction design, not the final stage.
n.4: Conversion is not one of the three core stages; integration is the last.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Why must manufacturers define target markets under product governance?
o: To ensure good outcomes and avoid foreseeable harm
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: Target market definition supports Consumer Duty and PROD by aligning products to needs and preventing foreseeable harm.

n.1: Maximising commission is not the objective, whereas preventing harm and delivering value is required.
n.2: Lower PI cost is incidental, while the core aim is outcomes and harm prevention.
n.3: Product governance complements suitability; it does not allow bypassing suitability obligations.
n.4: Disclosure simplification is not the purpose; the requirement centres on outcomes and value.

Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.q: Which legislation criminalises terrorist financing in the UK?
Regulatory Framework Principles & Rules.w: The Terrorism Act 2000 criminalises terrorist financing, including failure to disclose knowledge or suspicion of terrorist-related funds.

n.1: POCA addresses proceeds of crime generally, not terrorism financing specifically.
